·

items.title: Capcom announces plans to transform its RE Engine into an 'AI-generation game engine'
items.author: Rick Lane
items.summary: Capcom has been on an historic run over the last few years, delivering hit after hit during a period when many other publishers are struggling to keep their
items.text:
Capcom has been on an historic run over the last few years, delivering hit after hit during a period when many other publishers are struggling to keep their heads above water. This year alone, Capcom has released Resident Evil: Requiem, Pragmata, and Onimusha: Way of the Sword, all of which landed to both critical acclaim and commercial success.

So now is obviously the perfect time to wade into the not-at-all controversial topic of AI-powered game development.

Yesterday, Capcom held its own tech conference titled "Capcom Open Conference RE: 2026" during which programmer Satoshi Ishida gave a talk detailing the company's future plans for its proprietary RE: Engine—which powers all the publisher's modern games. During this talk, Ishida revealed Capcom's intentions to gradually transform RE Engine into an "AI-generation game engine."

Now, it's important to stress here that what Capcom appears to mean here is an engine for the AI generation, rather than a generative AI engine. As reported by Gamebiz (via IGN), Capcom's plans are more nuanced and detailed than slapping ChatGPT into its game development workflows.

During the talk, Ishida stated that the project is called "REX", and it involves six different programs that will integrate AI and machine-learning technology into RE Engine. Some of these are designed for enhancing program performance during development. Re:Dox, for example, is a data handling program designed to translate different types of data into a common set of rules for faster processing, while RE:UI is built to provide AI-assisted optimisation the RE: engine's development tools—sort-of like adding DLSS support for Blender.

Alongside these are tools designed to make the process of game development itself faster. There's a program called RE: Runtime, which apparently allows the engine to animate large numbers of objects and characters in groups—rather than running those real-time animations individually. Most intriguing is RE: Flows. This is apparently designed to simplify the implementation of game mechanic ideas, then convert them into a standardised programming language. This sounds vibe coding-adjacent to me, though it's hard to say for certain without seeing it in action.

According to Gamebiz, Capcom says it wants to integrate all these ideas into RE Engine for several reasons. First, modern games are so massive and technically complex that data management is a huge challenge and making changes to that data takes a long time. Second, more than 2,000 people now use RE Engine, including people from many different nationalities, so Capcom wants to create a system that is universally understandable. Third, AI technology is rapidly evolving and is essential for streamlining development—a somewhat arbitrary justification that I'm not convinced by.

Broadly though, these plans fall in line with Capcom's previously declared stance on AI, where the publisher stated it "will not implement assets generated by AI into our game content", but would use it to "enhance efficiency and boost productivity" in its development pipeline. Certainly, none of these tools appear designed to create art or character models and so forth, though it seems like some of them would require AI generated or AI assisted code to function.

It's also worth noting that Capcom's approach to development has worked pretty well for it over the last ten years, earning a reputation as one of the most reliable developers around. While I can understand the desire to make game development faster and more efficient, as the old adage goes, "If it ain't broke, don't fix it".

items.author: Angharad Redden

items.text:
PlayStation Plus Users Officially Have Until October 6 To Claim 4 Free Games

Published Oct 5, 2026, 5:26 AM EDT

Known as 'Cyberpunk 2077's' biggest fan, Angharad is a Welsh games writer who thrives in anything related to digital storytelling. If a video game explores the intricacies and horrors of womanhood, she is there.
Thanks to previous work at GAMINGbible, GameByte, The Loadout, Game Luster, Angharad has built a strong understanding of both the digital world and what fans want from it and is eager to share her thoughts and expertise with readers.

With the next batch of PlayStation Plus titles expected to go live on 6 October, you have only 24 hours to claim some previous additions. Ranging from a 2025 tactical shooter to a story-driven JRPG, there is something for everyone, and even if you do not yet want to play them, adding them to your library will ensure that you will have them available when the mood strikes you. Not only that, but following the removal of these games, three new titles are expected to join the service.

Set to leave the PlayStation Plus library at 08:00AM UTC on 6 October are:

Sniper Elite: Resistance (PS5/PS4)

MLB the Show 26 (PS5)

Wobbly Life (PS5/PS4)

Chained Echoes (PS4)

Sniper Elite: Resistance is a 2025 third-person tactical shooter and just another installment in the long-running Sniper Elite franchise. In this entry, players can expect "unparalleled sniping mechanics, stealth and tactical combat" with the story turning to a hidden war, far from the front lines, deep within the heart of an occupied France. Despite receiving somewhat mixed reviews at launch, Sniper Elite: Resistance still boasts a relatively positive review score a year on.

As for MLB the Show 26, the latest installment in the baseball video game series welcomes brand-new legends to the fray in the most immersive experience yet. As the official synopsis reads, "Discover improved Road To The Show mechanics, deeper Franchise experiences, thrilling Diamond Dynasty modes, enhanced customization options and true-to-life on-field action."

Wobbly Life is a vibrant, open-world physics sandbox experience to be played with friends online or in local co-op. With exciting jobs, mini-games, and wild story missions, you will be able to cause a whole lot of chaos and use your cash on clothes, vehicles, and houses. GTA VI, who?

Last, but by no means least, is Chained Echoes, a story-driven JRPG which tells the story of a group of heroes who must bring an end to the war between the three kingdoms of Valandis. In this 16-bit style RPG, players can expect an epic RPG set in a world "where dragons are as common as piloted mechanical suits."

As mentioned, these four titles are expected to leave the PlayStation Plus service in less than 24 hours. However, that means that they will make way for brand-new additions, including:

EA Sports F1 25 (PS5)

Hunt: Showdown 1896 (PS5)

Earth Defense Force: World Brothers 2 (PS5/PS4)

Featuring a racing title, an epic first-person extraction shooter, and a charming third-person shooter, the new additions feature something for everybody.

It is also worth mentioning that once it has left the PlayStation Plus Monthly Games Line-Up, Sniper Elite: Resistance will be added to the standard Game Catalog, so although it will only be available at its full price, it will still be accessible for those who missed out.

items.title: RetroSpace offers a huge sci-fi playground for inquisitive space janitors, but I'm not that System Shocked by the tools at your disposal
items.author: Edwin Evans-Thirlwell
items.summary: In my time as a videogame partaker, I have crawled through approximately three billion airvents. I may well have crawled through more vents than you've had hot
items.text:
In my time as a videogame partaker, I have crawled through approximately three billion airvents. I may well have crawled through more vents than you've had hot dinners. As such, any videogame that can get me excited about loosening a barred hatch and hauling my heavy ass into a square tunnel is doing something right.

The Wild Gentlemen's new sci-fi immersive sim RetroSpace gives pretty fair vent. It hides them all over. You'll walk along a dilapidated, meandering corridor and your eye will be caught by a certain combination of shadows, flirtatiously screened by pipes. 'Can I fit behind there?' You ask yourself, and lo, you have revealed a shortcut to the head engineer's office. Elsewhere, switches peek from behind stacks of luggable crates, and bent guard-rails draw your eye to a footwide ledge leading around the next pillar.

In general, RetroSpace does a nice job of squirrelling secrets into even the smallest chambers, and if the secret is very often a "rocket doughnut" or other inventory-clogging flotsam, sensing the prize and snuffling after it is a thrill. I hope the thrill will intensify as RetroSpace goes on, perhaps leaving a few of its obvious influences behind.

Watch on YouTube

RetroSpace takes place aboard Aurora 5, a pseudo-1970s interstellar ark that has tumbled into a black hole, and somehow come away with a mild case of temporal indecision – certain areas flip between timeframes - rather than spaghettification and incomprehensible doom. You are a janitor, woken from cryo to find a lot of stuff on fire, a lot of people dead, and a lot of other people deranged and monsterfied by gene-modding. Taking up your power wrench, you set out for the habitat hub and soon become embroiled in missions assigned by a handful of coherent survivors, including a sentient AI and a talking pig fellah.

These take you out to the far corners of the space station, which is very much the main character here. There's a "garden" sector that consists of a verdant silo with a starry dome, its spiral stairs and crawlspaces leading down to what I think is a bubbling soup of fertiliser. There's a train that circles the whole facility – not a camouflaged loading screen, as with chapter breaks in Dead Space, but an actual monorail car that travels in real time. There are a lot of audiologs, hackable terminals, and comedy public safety signs or adverts. As you might expect from the devisers of chicken detective games, RetroSpace skews toward caricature, which can get obnoxious – there's an audiolog early on that pokes fun at NPCs who leave scary audiologs. Still, it feels like the devs are fundamentally committed to making an engrossing world.

There's a persistent mystique woven around the station's janitors. Propaganda posters cast you and your lost brethren as urban legends, seldom seen by regular folk because you're always up a ladder or behind a bulkhead doing whatever it is you helmeted weirdos do with those sprays and spanners. Each sector has a locked or concealed utility closet with a portal to the Janitor's Haven - an interdimensional hideaway set up by union organisers, where you'll hang out with story-critical NPCs and do the bulk of your upgrading and customising.

If the station is a peach, I'm a little less convinced so far by the tools at your disposal. On the one hand, you've got weapons such as pistols, shotguns, and rayguns, all (eventually) upgradeable. On the other, you've got more indirect or tactical accessories such as cloaking devices, computer-hacking gizmos, and propulsive fire extinguishers. On the third hand, you've got genetic engineering or Mutamods, which range from giving yourself grasshopper thighs for higher jumping, moth ears so that you heal in light, or biceps full of rhino DNA for meatier clobbering.

The gene-modding cuts both ways: when you die, you'll be cloned for free at the nearest Bacta tank equivalent, but you'll be saddled with a random cartoon affliction for your troubles. I came away from one misadventure with a body prone to uncontrollable sneezing and swearing, which did not help with subsequent attempts at stealth. Fortunately, you can purge the debuffs by siphoning genetic material from the nearest vanilla human corpse, and Aurora 5 has no shortage of those.

Within the world, you can also do things like hold up crates to block bullets, or spray paths of water to create an electricity trap before smacking a circuit box. I'm really hoping that somewhere in RetroSpace, there lurks a tool or combination of tools that is as daft in its own way as Prey's Mimic ability. Or the slapstick bullshit you get in Skin Deep.

items.author: Clint Worthington

items.text:
It’s funny, looking back on 2026, that we’ll have gotten two televisual glimpses into the mind of the late, great chef and food writer Anthony Bourdain. One, Matt Johnson’s wry, tender biopic “Tony,” gives us a glimpse of the man’s larval form, the insecure, manipulative boy before he became the Tony we all knew and loved. The other? Bizarrely enough, an adaptation of a graphic novel he co-wrote in which a beleaguered chef with a checkered past punches, kicks, and decapitates his way (Casey Ryback-style) through a post-apocalyptic dystopia where haute cuisine carries enough cultural weight that people will kill for the right dish.

That’s the logline for “Get Jiro,” a graphic novel Bourdain penned in 2012 alongside Joel Rose, now adapted into a ten-episode Adult Swim series. The premise is so high-concept as to feel derivative, like a gumbo with too many disparate ingredients thrown together: In a resource-scarce future Los Angeles in which the populace entertains themselves with virtual reality, the only true sensory delights lie in food. Ergo, chefs have been elevated to a place of extreme cultural importance, mastering their craft like samurai and living like mob kingpins.

Living and cooking on the “Outer Ring” of this world is Jiro (Brian Tee), a stoic, unassuming sushi chef who, in the first episode, is approached by a sniveling dilettante at his humble locale to recruit him for greater things. But when the man insists on dipping his nigiri in soy sauce, Jiro’s blade gets another use besides slicing salmon, and the man’s head leaves his body. Unfortunately for Jiro, that becomes the first blow in a turf war that eventually sees him pitting two over-the-top rival chef kingpins, “Zatoichi”-style, against each other.

Get Jiro (Adult Swim)

All the components are there for a delightfully zany, bloody take on the yakuza/mob action thriller, with dishes as coveted as territory. But the original comic’s appeal lay in its vivid, grotesque artwork (by Langdon Foss) and the bona fides Bourdain’s name gave to its chef-flavored mayhem more than its story; Adult Swim’s adaptation loses the flavor of that artwork, dousing its well-worn cliches in unpalatable animation that feels more Flash animation than flashy.

Over the course of the first season’s ten episodes, Jiro is drawn further and further into the Inner Ring’s criminal underworld, battled over by Bob (Titus Welliver), a gruff, uncompromising maker of French international cuisine, and Rose (Allison Pill), a crunchy vegan who prides herself on ethical eating and no meat-is-murder dishes…though dispatching humans is a different story. Each wants Jiro’s talents with a blade (in any context) for their own reasons, and he’s more than happy to play them against each other, even as deeper scars from his family past begin to surface.

Granted, the show appeals most when it leans into the food-themed action: sniper-bakers who snuggle their rifle components in a series of baguettes, car chases evading variously themed food-truck bounty hunters, mob bosses drowning failed subordinates through what can only be described as “hollandaise-boarding.” The list goes on. Bourdain’s aim with the comic was clearly to send up the self-seriousness of chefs like himself, mixed with his love of samurai and yakuza movies, by building a fictional world where the tools and terms of chef culture become bloody weapons. Picture any “John Wick”-style action sequence set in a restaurant kitchen, and you get “Get Jiro”‘s whole deal.

Get Jiro (Adult Swim)

But after a few episodes, the novelty of the premise dissipates, and it gets harder to invest in the series’ twists and turns. As a character, Jiro remains pretty thin, his ronin-like stoicism buoyed mostly by the gradual reveal of his checkered past. His supporting cast offers little to offset that bitter taste; his allies consist of the well-meaning cop (Courtney Taylor) with her own relationship to food, and two innocent sisters (Seychelle Gabriel, Tessa Inez) whose proximity to Jiro put them in danger, most of whom don’t get enough to do to offset those formulaic roles.

The big later-show curveball comes in Justin Kirk‘s Alister, a Bourdain-like food critic whose relationship to Jiro’s cooking takes bizarre turns (especially after an episode featuring a violent escape from Butcher’s Block Prison, where all the big scary chefs get locked up). While the show mostly uses food as window dressing to add some seasoning to its been-there-done-that crime thriller action, Alister’s thread lets “Get Jiro” do what it does best: It actually explores our relationship to food and its various class signifiers.

It’s clear that shows like “Invincible” and “Blue Eye Samurai” have paved the way for something like “Get Jiro” to get made, and the animation style tries its level best to bring its over-the-top world to life. It’s clear showrunner Nate Cash (an old hand at “SpongeBob” and the director behind the brilliant “Over the Garden Wall”) had an uphill battle adapting this material for television, and it’s easy to relish the courses that feel pleasant on the tongue. If only the meal itself didn’t feel quite so bland.

All episodes screened for review. Premieres October 3rd on Adult Swim.

Marvel's 'Blade' Reboot Officially Finds a New Contender [Exclusive]

Image via New Line Cinema/courtesy Everett Collection

There have been many Marvel projects that have never seen the light of day, but none of them sting quite as profoundly as the MCU's Blade reboot. When Marvel first announced that Oscar winner Mahershala Ali would be stepping into the role of everyone's favorite vampire-hunting daywalker, there was a huge amount of excitement, especially considering that Blade hasn't gotten his own standalone movie since 2004. Despite having a very small voice cameo in a post-credits scene of Eternals, Ali has made it agonizingly clear that he is done waiting to play the character. MCU fans did get a consolation prize with Wesley Snipes reprising his iconic role in Deadpool & Wolverine, but despite his insistence that "There's only ever gonna be one Blade," one can't help but wonder what could have been with the scrapped reboot.

Perhaps Blade will get his time to shine in the MCU one day, bar his multiversal role in Marvel Zombies, but until then, a new contender to potentially replace Wesley Snipes and Mahershala Ali has thrown his hat into the ring. At a recent Q&A screening of the Friday the 13th prequel series Crystal Lake, hosted by Collider's Perri Nemiroff, series creator Bob Caleb Kane and star William Catlett were in attendance to dish on the behind-the-scenes secrets of the new Linda Cardellini-led show. Catlett is already a horror veteran thanks to the vampire flick Abigail, and it doesn't sound like he's ready to stop fighting the blood-sucking menaces just yet. When asked what was on his "horror moviemaking bucket list," Catlett was reluctant to respond, but eventually admitted he "wouldn't mind" playing Blade, which was met with a hugely positive response from both the crowd in attendance and Kane:

"I worked with Wesley [Snipes]. I don't know why they couldn't make it happen, but that’s something I would like to do."

REVEAL MY POWER →

The Gift Is Given
Your Power Is…

Four powers, and four completely different kinds of person behind them.
Here is what you would wake up with, what it would cost you, and why the MCU keeps handing it to
somebody exactly like you.

Hulk · Marvel Studios · Since 2008

Super Strength

You get the power that is really about taking the hit so that
nobody else has to. Strength in the MCU always lands on people who were already carrying too
much, which is exactly why it suits you.

Your instinct is to put yourself between the problem and the people, and you do it
before anybody has thought to ask.

Bruce Banner is the most interesting version of this because his story was never about
lifting things, it was about control.

The catch with strength is that people stop checking whether you are alright, since you
have made a habit of looking like you always are.

You would be the one everybody calls at two in the morning, and you would answer every
single time.

Spider-Man · Marvel Studios · Since 2016

Spider-Sense

You get the power that never switches off. Spider-sense is a gift
and a nervous system on permanent alert, and the people who get it in these films are always
the ones who were already worrying about everybody.

You read a situation faster than you can explain it, and you are usually right in a way
you cannot show your working for.

Peter Parker is the template because he takes on more than he can hold and then
apologises for not holding it well enough.

Spider-Man: Brand New Day arrived in July 2026 and put him back to being local, broke
and permanently on call.

The cost here is real, since a power that warns you about everything also means you are
never quite off duty.

The Fantastic Four · Marvel Studios · 2025

Invisibility

You get the quietest power in the building, and quietly the most
useful. Invisibility comes with force fields for a reason, because the people who prefer not
to be seen are usually the ones holding a shield around everybody else.

You notice everything, largely because you spend more time observing a room than
performing in it.

Sue Storm is the strongest member of her team and the least interested in anybody saying
so, which is very much your energy.

The Fantastic Four: First Steps finally gave the family a proper MCU home in 2025 and
made her the centre of it.

Your risk is that being unseen becomes a habit rather than a choice, and the people who
love you would like a look in.

Scarlet Witch · Marvel Studios · Since 2015

Chaos Magic

You get the biggest and least comfortable power on the list, the
one that runs directly on feeling. Chaos magic is not really a superpower in the MCU so much
as an emotional state with consequences attached.

You feel things at a volume other people do not, and you have spent years managing that
rather than being managed by it.

Wanda is the best written character Marvel has, precisely because her power and her
grief turned out to be the same thing.

WandaVision remains the high point of Marvel television, and it works because the
spectacle is only ever a symptom.

The warning attached to this one is simple. A power that answers to how you feel is only
ever as steady as you are.

Hopefully Catlett's dream of playing Blade comes true, but until then, he faces a totally different kind of threat as the sheriff of a small notorious town known as Crystal Lake in Peacock's new original series. Taking place years before the events of the original 1980 film, Crystal Lake sees Linda Cardellini as a young Pamela Voorhees as she tries to cope with the disappearance and presumed death of her son Jason (Callum Vinson). Hulk · Marvel Studios · Since 2008
Super Strength

You get the power that is really about taking the hit so that
nobody else has to. Strength in the MCU always lands on people who were already carrying too
much, which is exactly why it suits you.

before anybody has thought to ask.

lifting things, it was about control.

have made a habit of looking like you always are.

Writing from the Chicagoland area in Illinois, Robert is an avid movie watcher and will take just about any excuse to find time to go to his local movie theaters. Robert graduated from Bradley University with degrees in Journalism and Game Design with a minor in Film Studies. Robert tries his best to keep up with all the latest movie releases, from those released in theaters to those released on streaming. While he doesn't always keep up with the latest TV shows, he makes it a goal to watch nearly every major new release possible. He has been honing his craft and following any and all movie news all his life, leading up to now, where he has a vast knowledge of film and film history. He also logs every movie that he watches on his Letterboxd page, and has hosted a weekly online movie night with his closest friends for over 6 years.

The 2000s were a defining decade when it came to feature-length animation as a whole. The decade saw the massive rise of 3D computer animation becoming the new standard in studio animation, and the decade as a whole saw more and more filmmakers use animation to experiment and tell their own beautiful stories. At the same time, the decade was also considered the final hurrah for 2D animation as the primary form of animation, acting as a sort of swan song before transitioning into the future of animated storytelling.

With so many groundbreaking and inspirational animated stories to be released during this time, every individual will have their own favorites and biases. Websites such as Letterboxd have been a helpful tool in being able to gather together user scores from their community in order to form a cohesive average ranking for each movie. From this, it is possible to see in finality exactly which animated films from the 2000s are held in the highest regard by the Letterboxd community.

15
'Mind Game' (2004)

Letterboxd Average Rating: 4.19/5

Image via Asmik Ace Entertainment

A display of sheer visual madness and absurdism in the medium of anime filmmaking, Mind Game is one of the most distinct and individual animated films out there, balancing insightful storytelling on the fluidity of life while maximizing the goofiness of its story and animation. Director Masaaki Yuasa fills the film with raw, unrestrained personality and charm in every second of its animation and filmmaking, creating an unmistakable work of art that could only work in the realm of animation.

The film follows Nishi, an awkward loser who ends up getting an unlikely second chance at life after he is murdered in an encounter with the Japanese mafia and runs his way back to the world of the living through sheer force of will. With a second chance at life, he acts unrestrained and chooses to never live in fear again, sending him and his friends on a mad car chase that leaves them stuck in the belly of a giant whale. The animation and comedy live up to the absurdity of its premise, making for an unforgettable animated experience that Letterboxd users have fallen in love with.

14
'Vampire Hunter D: Bloodlust' (2000)

Letterboxd Average Rating: 4.19/5

Image via Madhouse/Nippon Herald Films

The original Vampire Hunter D was already an icon of gothic anime filmmaking, yet releasing 15 years after the original film, Vampire Hunter D: Bloodlust expands and elevates the strengths of the original into the legendary digital era with seamless precision. It sees the titular D on yet another vampire-hunting quest, competing with a family of bounty hunters to track down a young woman who has seemingly been abducted by the notorious vampire nobleman Meier Link.

With a masterful visual style and gothic set pieces, Vampire Hunter D: Bloodlust brilliantly executes upon the concepts and worldbuilding established in the original film, creating a striking masterwork of R-rated anime that has been celebrated as a champion of the art form since its release. The exceptional style of legendary anime director Yoshiaki Kawajiri is arguably at its best in this masterclass of dark anime.

13
'Coraline' (2009)

Letterboxd Average Rating: 4.19/5

Image via Focus Features

The absolute face of stop-motion animation mastery in the 21st century is animation studio LAIKA, whose various works of beauty have been celebrated as some of the best stop-motion movies ever made. The undeniable highlight of their legendary filmography, however, is Coraline, a beautifully dark story of fantastical worlds and the harsh truth of idealized fantasies. The film follows the titular 11-year-old girl as she discovers a hidden door to a strange, alternate version of her own world that seems perfect, yet requires a haunting sacrifice for her to stay.

Coraline is an experience defined by the beauty and sheer impressive stature of its visuals that still hold up tremendously over 15 years after its release. With titan of stop-motion animation Henry Selick at the helm, Coraline is one of the most beautifully crafted stop-motion animated films ever made, which is all the more impactful thanks to the brilliance of its storytelling and the charm of its characters.

12
'Azur & Asmar: The Princes' Quest' (2006)

Letterboxd Average Rating: 4.20/5

Image via GKIDS

Defined by its beautifully distinct folklore art style and storytelling, Azur & Asmar: The Princes' Quest is some of the closest that an original film in the 21st century has gotten to recreating the magic and joy of the timeless fairy tales of old. The French film follows the young Azur and his best friend, who was separated from him in childhood, Asmar, as they both independently travel to North Africa in search of the legendary djinn-fairy in hopes of marrying her.

The striking visual style of the film, which utilizes 3D technology to create a wholly distinct 2D world, is the major highlight of the film. However, the brilliance of its timeless story has also played a great deal into the film's lasting appeal and legacy as one of the best French animated films ever made. It's a work of art that still feels brilliantly crafted 20 years after its release as an incredibly underrated icon of independent 3D animated films.

11
'Ratatouille' (2007)

Letterboxd Average Rating: 4.22/5

Image via Walt Disney Studios Motion Pictures

Ratatouille tells the story of Remy, a rat who has extravagant dreams of becoming a great French chef, yet is faced with the obvious hurdle of being a rat, an animal notoriously not allowed in kitchens. However, thanks to a chance encounter and partnership with the kind-hearted Linguini, Remy is finally given his chance to prove himself as a great chef in a restaurant made famous by Remy's own hero.

Ratatouille is a symbolic representation of all the best aspects of Pixar's core filmmaking attributes and style wrapped up in a singular near-perfect package. The film's powerful yet simple message of "anyone can cook" is as timeless as it gets, and the film's emotional beats and humor still connect with audiences over 15 years later. In the eyes of the Letterboxd community, Ratatouille is one of the greatest films that Pixar has made, and it will be a long time before a film is able to come close to its overwhelming quality.

10
'Persepolis' (2007)

Letterboxd Average Rating: 4.23/5

Image via Diaphana Distribution

Persepolis tells the story of Marji, a young woman growing up in the harsh environment of 1970s Iran, firsthand experiencing the Iranian Revolution of 1979 and the new Islamic rulership. While Marji and her family have high hopes for the possibilities of the revolution and a new leadership, they soon come to realize that the new rulers have become a new form of repressive tyranny in itself.

Adapted directly from the famous graphic novel series, Persepolis is able to perfectly translate the original visual style of the graphic novel into animation while still keeping its core adult themes and messages. The film uses its stylized animation style as an excellent low barrier to entry for the harsh and powerful coming-of-age story at its center, allowing its important tale to be reached and more accessible across the world.

9
'Millennium Actress' (2001)

Letterboxd Average Rating: 4.24/5

Image via Madhouse

Millennium Actress follows the story of legendary actress Chiyoko Fujiwara, who vanished at the height of her career but has now been tracked down by a documentary filmmaker looking to tell her story to the world. As her story unfolds, the line between fiction and reality becomes blurrier and blurrier as her real-life experiences are told through the movies that were a part of her extensive career. Her story reveals a great deal of secrets about why she went into hiding, why she began acting in the first place, and even an unexpected connection to the documentarian's past.

Millennium Actress uses an incredibly unique and unexpected method of telling its mature and multilayered story of legacy and love, as it plays with visuals and locations constantly in a way that perfectly fits the character of Chiyoko. Even with the scattered way that it tells its story, it all converges perfectly in the end in a glorious sendoff that tells the power and drive that love can have in your life, and how life gives back into that love. The film is a genuine work of art that is frankly nothing more than the standard for legendary director Satoshi Kon.

Collider Exclusive · Oscar Best Picture Quiz
Which Oscar Best Picture
Is Your Perfect Movie?
Parasite · Everything Everywhere · Oppenheimer · Birdman · No Country

Five Oscar Best Picture winners. Five completely different visions of what cinema can be — and what it can do to you. One of them is the film that was made for the way your mind works. Ten questions will figure out which one.

🪜Parasite

🌀Everything Everywhere

☢️Oppenheimer

🐦Birdman

🪙No Country for Old Men

FIND YOUR FILM →

01

What kind of film experience do you actually want?
The best movies don't just entertain — they leave something behind.

ASomething that pulls the rug out — that makes me think I'm watching one kind of film and then reveals I'm watching another entirely.
BSomething overwhelming — funny, sad, absurd, and genuinely moving, all at once.
CSomething grand and weighty — a film that makes me feel the full scale of what I'm watching.
DSomething formally daring — a film that pushes what cinema can even do.
ESomething lean and relentless — pure tension with no wasted frame.

NEXT QUESTION →

02

Which idea grabs you most in a film?
Great films are driven by a central obsession. What's yours?

AClass, inequality, and what people are willing to do when desperation meets opportunity.
BIdentity, family, and the chaos of trying to hold your life together when everything is falling apart.
CGenius, moral responsibility, and the catastrophic weight of a decision you can never take back.
DEgo, legacy, and the terror of becoming irrelevant while you're still alive to watch it happen.
EEvil, chance, and whether moral order actually exists or if we just tell ourselves it does.

NEXT QUESTION →

03

How do you like your story told?
Form is content. The way a story is shaped changes what it means.

AGenre-twisting — I want it to start in one lane and migrate into something completely different.
BMaximalist and genre-blending — comedy, action, drama, sci-fi, all in one ride.
CEpic and non-linear — cutting between timelines, building a mosaic of cause and consequence.
DA single unbroken flow — I want to feel like I'm living it in real time, no cuts to safety.
ESpare and precise — every scene doing exactly what it needs to do and nothing more.

NEXT QUESTION →

04

What makes a truly great antagonist?
The opposition defines the protagonist. What kind of opposition fascinates you?

AA system — invisible, structural, and almost impossible to fight because it has no single face.
BThe self — the ways we sabotage, abandon, and fail the people we love most.
CHistory — the unstoppable momentum of events that no single person can stop or redirect.
DThe industry — the machinery of culture that chews up talent and spits out irrelevance.
EPure, implacable evil — a force so certain of itself it becomes almost philosophical.

NEXT QUESTION →

05

What do you want from a film's ending?
The final note is the one that lingers. What do you want it to sound like?

AShock and inevitability — a conclusion that recontextualises everything that came before it.
BEarned emotion — I want to cry, laugh, and feel genuinely hopeful, even if the world is a mess.
CDevastation and grandeur — an ending that makes me sit in silence for a few minutes after.
DAmbiguity — something that leaves enough open that I'm still thinking about it days later.
EBleakness — an honest refusal to pretend the world is tidier than it actually is.

NEXT QUESTION →

06

Which setting pulls you in most?
Where a film takes place shapes everything — mood, stakes, what's even possible.

AA gleaming modern city with a hidden underside — beauty masking rot, wealth masking desperation.
BA collapsing suburban life that opens onto something infinite — the multiverse of a single ordinary person.
CThe corridors of power and science at a world-historical turning point — where decisions echo for decades.
DThe grimy, alive chaos of New York and Hollywood — fame as both destination and trap.
EVast, indifferent landscape — desert and highway where violence arrives without warning or reason.

NEXT QUESTION →

07

What cinematic craft impresses you most?
Every great film has a signature — a technical or artistic element that makes it unmistakable.

AProduction design and mise-en-scène — every frame composed to carry meaning beneath the surface.
BEditing and tonal control — the ability to move between registers without losing the audience.
CScore and sound design — music that becomes inseparable from the dread and awe of what you're watching.
DCinematography as performance — the camera not recording events but participating in them.
ESilence and restraint — what's left unsaid and unshown doing more work than any dialogue could.

NEXT QUESTION →

08

What kind of main character do you root for?
The protagonist is the lens. Who you choose to follow says something about you.

ASomeone smart and resourceful who makes increasingly dangerous decisions under pressure.
BSomeone overwhelmed and ordinary who turns out to be capable of something extraordinary.
CA brilliant, tortured figure whose gifts and flaws are inseparable from each other.
DA self-destructive artist whose ego is both their superpower and their undoing.
EA quiet, principled person trying to make sense of a world that has stopped making sense.

NEXT QUESTION →

09

How do you feel about a film that takes its time?
Pace is a choice. Some films sprint; others let tension accumulate slowly, deliberately.

AI love a slow build when I know the payoff is going to be seismic — patience for a devastating reveal.
BGive me relentless momentum — I want to feel breathless and emotionally spent by the end.
CEpic runtime doesn't scare me — if the material demands three hours, give me three hours.
DI want it to feel propulsive even when nothing is technically happening — restless energy throughout.
EDeliberate and unhurried — I want dread to accumulate in the spaces between the action.

NEXT QUESTION →

10

What do you want to feel walking out of the cinema?
The best films leave a mark. What kind of mark do you want?

AUnsettled — like I've just seen something I can't fully explain but can't stop thinking about.
BMoved and energised — like the film reminded me what actually matters and gave me something to hold onto.
CHumbled — like I've been in the presence of something genuinely important and overwhelming.
DExhilarated — like I've just seen cinema doing something it's never quite done before.
EHaunted — like a cold, quiet dread that stays with me for days.

REVEAL MY FILM →

The Academy Has Decided
Your Perfect Film Is…

Your answers have pointed to one Oscar Best Picture winner above all others. This is the film that was made for the way your mind works.

Parasite

You are drawn to films that operate on multiple levels simultaneously — that begin in one genre and quietly, brilliantly migrate into another. Bong Joon-ho's Parasite is a film about class, desire, and the architecture of inequality that manages to be darkly funny, deeply suspenseful, and genuinely shocking across a single extraordinary running time. Your instinct is for cinema that hides its true intentions until the moment it's ready to reveal them. Parasite is exactly that — a film that rewards close attention and punishes assumptions, right up to its devastating final image.

Everything Everywhere All at Once

You want it all — and this film gives you all of it. The Daniels' Everything Everywhere All at Once is one of the most maximalist films ever made: action comedy, multiverse sci-fi, family drama, existential crisis, and a genuinely earned emotional core that sneaks up on you amid the chaos. You are someone who responds to ambition, who doesn't want cinema to choose between being entertaining and being meaningful. This film refuses that choice entirely. It is overwhelming by design, and its overwhelming nature is precisely the point — because the feeling of being crushed by infinite possibility is exactly what it's about.

Oppenheimer

You are drawn to cinema on a grand scale — films that understand history not as a backdrop but as a force, and that place their characters inside that force and watch what happens. Christopher Nolan's Oppenheimer is a film about the terrifying gap between what we can do and what we should do, told with the full weight of one of the most consequential moments in human history behind it. You want your films to feel important without feeling self-important — to earn their ambition through sheer craft and the gravity of their subject. Oppenheimer does exactly that. It is enormous, complicated, and refuses easy comfort.

Birdman

You are drawn to films that foreground their own construction — that make the how of the filmmaking part of the what it's about. Alejandro González Iñárritu's Birdman, shot to appear as a single continuous take, is cinema examining itself through the cracked mirror of a fading actor's ego. You respond to formal daring, to the feeling that a film is doing something that probably shouldn't be possible. Michael Keaton's performance and Emmanuel Lubezki's restless camera create something genuinely unlike anything else — a film that is simultaneously about creativity, relevance, self-destruction, and the impossibility of ever truly knowing if your work means anything at all.

No Country for Old Men

You are drawn to cinema that trusts silence, that refuses to explain itself, and that treats dread as a form of meaning. The Coen Brothers' No Country for Old Men is a film about the arrival of a new kind of evil — implacable, arbitrary, and utterly indifferent to the moral frameworks we use to make sense of the world. It is one of the most formally controlled films ever made, and its controlled restraint is what makes it so terrifying. You want your films to haunt you, not comfort you. You are not interested in resolution if resolution would be dishonest. No Country for Old Men is honest in a way that most cinema never dares to be.

↻ RETAKE THE QUIZ

8
'WALL-E' (2008)

Letterboxd Average Rating: 4.24/5

Image via Pixar Animation

WALL-E tells the story of Wall-E, the last remaining robot left on Earth tasked with cleaning up all of the garbage that has been left behind after humans fled to the far reaches of outer space 700 years ago. When a brand-new ship arrives on Earth containing a new, more modernistic robot, Wall-E believes that he may have finally found his first real friend in 700 years.

Pixar's track record in the 2000s cannot be overstated, yet Wall-E still stands as one of the studio's greatest artistic accomplishments, telling a beautiful, heartwarming story of romance and the environment. The film holds an outstanding and everlasting legacy 15 years later, even standing alone as the only Pixar movie to earn a spot in the Criterion Collection.

7
'Tokyo Godfathers' (2003)

Letterboxd Average Rating: 4.26/5

Image via Sony Pictures Entertainment Japan

Satoshi Kon's Tokyo Godfathers tells the story of a trio of homeless people living in Tokyo on Christmas Eve: the middle-aged alcoholic, Gin, the former drag queen, Hana, and the runaway girl, Miyuki. The trio soon faces a conundrum when they discover an abandoned newborn baby while searching through the garbage, and with only a handful of clues at their disposal, they decide to search the city for the infant's parents.

Despite its darker premise, Tokyo Godfathers is perfectly able to conjure the magical feelings of the holiday season, and the power and strength of familial bonds that can come from anywhere. The charming connection and chemistry between all three of the leads create an infectious feeling of warmth that can't help but envelop audiences in its sense of comfort. Even 20 years later, the film still has a lot of powerful notions to say about the holidays and the importance of being interconnected even under the worst of conditions.

6
'Mary and Max' (2009)

Letterboxd Average Rating: 4.27/5

Image via Icon Entertainment International

Mary and Max tells the tale of friendship between the unlikely pen pals of Mary, a lonely eight-year-old girl living in the suburbs of Melbourne, and Max, an obese 44-year-old man living in New York. While their friendship started from humble beginnings, with Mary picking a name out of a phone book and writing a letter, their friendship would soon go on to last 20 years, with both of their lives changing drastically in that time.

Sporting a beautiful clay animation style, Mary and Max is able to use its childish and seemingly simplistic visual style to tell a highly mature and powerful tale of friendship and the human spirit. The acclaimed claymation film also accomplishes this thanks to its all-star casting of Toni Collette as Mary and Philip Seymour Hoffman as Max, who both bring their A-game and bring life to the characters of Mary and Max.

It sees the titular D on yet another vampire-hunting quest, competing with a family of bounty hunters to track down a young woman who has seemingly been abducted by the notorious vampire nobleman Meier Link.

With a masterful visual style and gothic set pieces, Vampire Hunter D: Bloodlust brilliantly executes upon the concepts and worldbuilding established in the original film, creating a striking masterwork of R-rated anime that has been celebrated as a champion of the art form since its release. The exceptional style of legendary anime director Yoshiaki Kawajiri is arguably at its best in this masterclass of dark anime.

'Coraline' (2009)
Letterboxd Average Rating: 4.19/5

The absolute face of stop-motion animation mastery in the 21st century is animation studio LAIKA, whose various works of beauty have been celebrated as some of the best stop-motion movies ever made. The undeniable highlight of their legendary filmography, however, is Coraline, a beautifully dark story of fantastical worlds and the harsh truth of idealized fantasies. The film follows the titular 11-year-old girl as she discovers a hidden door to a strange, alternate version of her own world that seems perfect, yet requires a haunting sacrifice for her to stay.

Coraline is an experience defined by the beauty and sheer impressive stature of its visuals that still hold up tremendously over 15 years after its release. With titan of stop-motion animation Henry Selick at the helm, Coraline is one of the most beautifully crafted stop-motion animated films ever made, which is all the more impactful thanks to the brilliance of its storytelling and the charm of its characters.

'Azur & Asmar: The Princes' Quest' (2006)
Letterboxd Average Rating: 4.20/5
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/three-people-at-a-dinner-table-in-azur-asmar-the-princes-quest.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1

blocks.x: Image via GKIDS

Defined by its beautifully distinct folklore art style and storytelling, Azur & Asmar: The Princes' Quest is some of the closest that an original film in the 21st century has gotten to recreating the magic and joy of the timeless fairy tales of old. The French film follows the young Azur and his best friend, who was separated from him in childhood, Asmar, as they both independently travel to North Africa in search of the legendary djinn-fairy in hopes of marrying her.

The striking visual style of the film, which utilizes 3D technology to create a wholly distinct 2D world, is the major highlight of the film. However, the brilliance of its timeless story has also played a great deal into the film's lasting appeal and legacy as one of the best French animated films ever made. It's a work of art that still feels brilliantly crafted 20 years after its release as an incredibly underrated icon of independent 3D animated films.

'Ratatouille' (2007)
Letterboxd Average Rating: 4.22/5

blocks.x: Image via Walt Disney Studios Motion Pictures

Ratatouille tells the story of Remy, a rat who has extravagant dreams of becoming a great French chef, yet is faced with the obvious hurdle of being a rat, an animal notoriously not allowed in kitchens. However, thanks to a chance encounter and partnership with the kind-hearted Linguini, Remy is finally given his chance to prove himself as a great chef in a restaurant made famous by Remy's own hero.

Ratatouille is a symbolic representation of all the best aspects of Pixar's core filmmaking attributes and style wrapped up in a singular near-perfect package. The film's powerful yet simple message of "anyone can cook" is as timeless as it gets, and the film's emotional beats and humor still connect with audiences over 15 years later. In the eyes of the Letterboxd community, Ratatouille is one of the greatest films that Pixar has made, and it will be a long time before a film is able to come close to its overwhelming quality.

'Persepolis' (2007)

Persepolis tells the story of Marji, a young woman growing up in the harsh environment of 1970s Iran, firsthand experiencing the Iranian Revolution of 1979 and the new Islamic rulership. While Marji and her family have high hopes for the possibilities of the revolution and a new leadership, they soon come to realize that the new rulers have become a new form of repressive tyranny in itself.

Adapted directly from the famous graphic novel series, Persepolis is able to perfectly translate the original visual style of the graphic novel into animation while still keeping its core adult themes and messages. The film uses its stylized animation style as an excellent low barrier to entry for the harsh and powerful coming-of-age story at its center, allowing its important tale to be reached and more accessible across the world.

'Millennium Actress' (2001)
Letterboxd Average Rating: 4.24/5

Millennium Actress follows the story of legendary actress Chiyoko Fujiwara, who vanished at the height of her career but has now been tracked down by a documentary filmmaker looking to tell her story to the world. As her story unfolds, the line between fiction and reality becomes blurrier and blurrier as her real-life experiences are told through the movies that were a part of her extensive career. Her story reveals a great deal of secrets about why she went into hiding, why she began acting in the first place, and even an unexpected connection to the documentarian's past.

Millennium Actress uses an incredibly unique and unexpected method of telling its mature and multilayered story of legacy and love, as it plays with visuals and locations constantly in a way that perfectly fits the character of Chiyoko. Even with the scattered way that it tells its story, it all converges perfectly in the end in a glorious sendoff that tells the power and drive that love can have in your life, and how life gives back into that love. The film is a genuine work of art that is frankly nothing more than the standard for legendary director Satoshi Kon.

Five Oscar Best Picture winners. Five completely different visions of what cinema can be — and what it can do to you. One of them is the film that was made for the way your mind works. Ten questions will figure out which one.

What kind of film experience do you actually want?
The best movies don't just entertain — they leave something behind.

ASomething that pulls the rug out — that makes me think I'm watching one kind of film and then reveals I'm watching another entirely.

Which idea grabs you most in a film?
Great films are driven by a central obsession. What's yours?

CGenius, moral responsibility, and the catastrophic weight of a decision you can never take back.

EEvil, chance, and whether moral order actually exists or if we just tell ourselves it does.

How do you like your story told?
Form is content. The way a story is shaped changes what it means.

AGenre-twisting — I want it to start in one lane and migrate into something completely different.
BMaximalist and genre-blending — comedy, action, drama, sci-fi, all in one ride.
CEpic and non-linear — cutting between timelines, building a mosaic of cause and consequence.
DA single unbroken flow — I want to feel like I'm living it in real time, no cuts to safety.
ESpare and precise — every scene doing exactly what it needs to do and nothing more.

What makes a truly great antagonist?
The opposition defines the protagonist. What kind of opposition fascinates you?

AA system — invisible, structural, and almost impossible to fight because it has no single face.
BThe self — the ways we sabotage, abandon, and fail the people we love most.
CHistory — the unstoppable momentum of events that no single person can stop or redirect.
DThe industry — the machinery of culture that chews up talent and spits out irrelevance.
EPure, implacable evil — a force so certain of itself it becomes almost philosophical.

What do you want from a film's ending?
The final note is the one that lingers. What do you want it to sound like?

AShock and inevitability — a conclusion that recontextualises everything that came before it.
BEarned emotion — I want to cry, laugh, and feel genuinely hopeful, even if the world is a mess.
CDevastation and grandeur — an ending that makes me sit in silence for a few minutes after.
DAmbiguity — something that leaves enough open that I'm still thinking about it days later.
EBleakness — an honest refusal to pretend the world is tidier than it actually is.

Which setting pulls you in most?

AA gleaming modern city with a hidden underside — beauty masking rot, wealth masking desperation.

CThe corridors of power and science at a world-historical turning point — where decisions echo for decades.

AProduction design and mise-en-scène — every frame composed to carry meaning beneath the surface.

CScore and sound design — music that becomes inseparable from the dread and awe of what you're watching.
DCinematography as performance — the camera not recording events but participating in them.
ESilence and restraint — what's left unsaid and unshown doing more work than any dialogue could.

ASomeone smart and resourceful who makes increasingly dangerous decisions under pressure.
BSomeone overwhelmed and ordinary who turns out to be capable of something extraordinary.
CA brilliant, tortured figure whose gifts and flaws are inseparable from each other.
DA self-destructive artist whose ego is both their superpower and their undoing.
EA quiet, principled person trying to make sense of a world that has stopped making sense.

How do you feel about a film that takes its time?

AI love a slow build when I know the payoff is going to be seismic — patience for a devastating reveal.
BGive me relentless momentum — I want to feel breathless and emotionally spent by the end.
CEpic runtime doesn't scare me — if the material demands three hours, give me three hours.

What do you want to feel walking out of the cinema?

AUnsettled — like I've just seen something I can't fully explain but can't stop thinking about.
BMoved and energised — like the film reminded me what actually matters and gave me something to hold onto.
CHumbled — like I've been in the presence of something genuinely important and overwhelming.
DExhilarated — like I've just seen cinema doing something it's never quite done before.
EHaunted — like a cold, quiet dread that stays with me for days.

The Academy Has Decided
Your Perfect Film Is…
Your answers have pointed to one Oscar Best Picture winner above all others. This is the film that was made for the way your mind works.
Parasite

You are drawn to films that operate on multiple levels simultaneously — that begin in one genre and quietly, brilliantly migrate into another. Bong Joon-ho's Parasite is a film about class, desire, and the architecture of inequality that manages to be darkly funny, deeply suspenseful, and genuinely shocking across a single extraordinary running time. Your instinct is for cinema that hides its true intentions until the moment it's ready to reveal them. Parasite is exactly that — a film that rewards close attention and punishes assumptions, right up to its devastating final image.
Everything Everywhere All at Once

You want it all — and this film gives you all of it. The Daniels' Everything Everywhere All at Once is one of the most maximalist films ever made: action comedy, multiverse sci-fi, family drama, existential crisis, and a genuinely earned emotional core that sneaks up on you amid the chaos. You are someone who responds to ambition, who doesn't want cinema to choose between being entertaining and being meaningful. This film refuses that choice entirely. It is overwhelming by design, and its overwhelming nature is precisely the point — because the feeling of being crushed by infinite possibility is exactly what it's about.
Oppenheimer

You are drawn to cinema on a grand scale — films that understand history not as a backdrop but as a force, and that place their characters inside that force and watch what happens. Christopher Nolan's Oppenheimer is a film about the terrifying gap between what we can do and what we should do, told with the full weight of one of the most consequential moments in human history behind it. You want your films to feel important without feeling self-important — to earn their ambition through sheer craft and the gravity of their subject. Oppenheimer does exactly that. It is enormous, complicated, and refuses easy comfort.
Birdman

You are drawn to films that foreground their own construction — that make the how of the filmmaking part of the what it's about. Alejandro González Iñárritu's Birdman, shot to appear as a single continuous take, is cinema examining itself through the cracked mirror of a fading actor's ego. You respond to formal daring, to the feeling that a film is doing something that probably shouldn't be possible. Michael Keaton's performance and Emmanuel Lubezki's restless camera create something genuinely unlike anything else — a film that is simultaneously about creativity, relevance, self-destruction, and the impossibility of ever truly knowing if your work means anything at all.
No Country for Old Men

You are drawn to cinema that trusts silence, that refuses to explain itself, and that treats dread as a form of meaning. The Coen Brothers' No Country for Old Men is a film about the arrival of a new kind of evil — implacable, arbitrary, and utterly indifferent to the moral frameworks we use to make sense of the world. It is one of the most formally controlled films ever made, and its controlled restraint is what makes it so terrifying. You want your films to haunt you, not comfort you. You are not interested in resolution if resolution would be dishonest. No Country for Old Men is honest in a way that most cinema never dares to be.

Sporting a beautiful clay animation style, Mary and Max is able to use its childish and seemingly simplistic visual style to tell a highly mature and powerful tale of friendship and the human spirit. items.text:
Disk Cleanup

(Image credit: Future)Welcome to Disk Cleanup, our regular weekend feature delving into the PCs of PC gaming luminaries. Come back every weekend to read a new interview, digging into the important questions, like "How tidy is your desktop?" and "What game will you never uninstall?"

Tonda Ros was first drawn to PC gaming at seven years old, after playing the action-adventure classic, Beast. "It's kind of like an open, nonlinear Sokoban that's action-based and not puzzle-based," says Ros, the creator of 2025's Blue Prince. "I think it was the next year where we had a 386 PC in the house, and that's when the floodgates opened … when I played Tank Wars and the original SimCity and Star Control."

Establishing a career as a cinematographer and visual artist, in 2016, Ros began working on Blue Prince. Inspired by games like Myst, board games like Jewels in the Attic and puzzle books like Maze: Solve the World's Most Challenging Puzzle, Blue Prince was painstakingly created across the best part of a decade. When it released last year, it quickly established itself as a modern puzzling classic.

After taking a break following Blue Prince's launch, Ros is currently working on tech support for the puzzler, while also experimenting with new projects. "I think the next game will have to be a smaller game, logistically," he says. But he stepped out of his game development lab to show me around the ever-shifting parlour of his Steam library.

What game are you currently playing?

(Image credit: The Game Bakers)I'm currently playing Cairn, by The Game Bakers, which is just a gorgeous rock-climbing simulator/adventure game with some survival elements. What's remarkable about the game is how much it feels like rock climbing, and how simple and intuitive the controls are.

I didn't even have to do a tutorial to understand, because that's just how simple and intuitive the controls are—where you control each limb in sequential order. It's just one of the most well-executed control schemes that I've ever seen. And it's not a control scheme that I had seen before.

I think what's really interesting to me is how similar the controls are, conceptually, to last year's Baby Steps, because these are both games where you're controlling individual limbs [and] climb up a mountainous terrain. But one is incredibly intuitive and smooth and frictionless—in the way the controls are executed at least. And then of course Baby Steps goes to the opposite side of the metric.

I love both games, and I think it's cool to see such similar design work conceptually, but with just slight tweaks in the game feel, they're completely different and unique experiences.

What was the previous game you played, and is it still installed?

(Image credit: Panic)That would be Big Walk, which is funny because that's also a game about climbing and walking. But yes, I just finished—two weeks ago—Big Walk with my group of friends, and that was an amazing experience.

I have been waiting for that game since it was announced at The Game Awards many years ago, and it's fascinating, because it's the first social proximity chat game I've ever played. I had been waiting for Big Walk for so long that every time other ones came up, I was like, "Yeah, I'd like to play this, but I'm waiting for Big Walk."

It's fascinating because they started development before this whole social chat scene kicked in. It reminds me a lot of Blue Prince, because I started Blue Prince's development before there were any deckbuilders. So you kind of get a sense that this is something that was created in parallel to those design trends, and you see the different decisions that they made, in the same way that I don't think Blue Prince really feels like a deck builder, though you could probably tell we share similar tabletop designs.

I played it with [seven] people. We had been prepped to play this for years … we played it on Thursdays and Sundays, Thursday was a shorter session and then Sunday was a little bit longer. And it was fun because seven people really allowed us to get lost in groups, where two people would be in a conversation and get distracted and fall away, and we wouldn't see them again for four hours. And that was exciting to me.

I don't want to spoil Big Walk for anyone that plays, but the ending just blew me away. I will say that it literally shook me. I think for a lot of times, I'm playing as a game designer, and you can't help but have a little design hat on where you're like "Oh, I would have done this differently" or "I think I could see ways that they could have improved this."

And when I played the last act of Big Walk, I was in awe, because there is no way I could have come to a fraction as good of an ending to that game, as the way they did. So hats off to House House, well deserved success.

What is the oldest game (by release date) currently installed on your PC?

I had thought it would be this, and I'm happy to report it's Myst, 1993. I have Cyan's entire catalogue installed. Myst will always be on my PC. It might not always be the oldest, but Myst is not one that's going anywhere.

There were many, many years where I just liked hanging out in that world, just to listen to the atmosphere while I was working. Hearing the wind and the oceans lap at the shore of Myst island. It has a serene quality. And it has a very deep familiarity because of how many years of my life were spent in that game as a kid, and especially [because] it was my first exposure to an immersive graphical world.

The very first time I played Myst was at a friend's house, and I was going to check out their Super Nintendo because they had just gotten [one] around the same time, and then he was like "Do you want to play something else?" And he took me to his father's office, who had a PC on his desk, and he booted it up, and I was just absolutely stunlocked … and I remember the day I got back, I told my parents—I didn't ask for a Super Nintendo—I told them "We need to get a computer with a CD-ROM."

I'm glad that my game and Big Walk and these games are finding success … because unlike a lot of other genres that are oversaturated, the first-person puzzle game is really not oversaturated. It's crazy, because you have Outer Wilds and Obra Dinn and all these games finding success and [being] universally beloved, and the community is ravenous for new experiences … I hope it encourages more people to explore these areas.

What is the highest number of hours you have in any given game, according to Steam?

(Image credit: Mossmouth)I'm only looking at Steam here, so thankfully I get to discount Battle.net, and I'm going to disqualify my own game. So the winner would be Mossmouth's magnificent UFO 50, clocking in at 691 hours. But I'm pretty sure a few hundred of those hours are because of Pilot Quest, which likely won't surprise anyone familiar with the game.

If you aren't familiar … UFO 50 is a collection of 50 games—so it's kind of a cheat in terms of the hours—that all belong to a fictional 1980s console called the LX. And if my hours of play are any indication, these are not 50 mini games. They're 50 games, full games that have a lot of depth, and they're as sizeable as any of the games from the '80s.

There are games across every genre. I remember when I first heard of it, I was like, "OK, that's a cool concept, [but] I don't really play a lot of retro nostalgia-driven games." But when I first saw a clip, the design work I was seeing was like, "Oh, they're doing some cool stuff." I think I saw a clip of one of the games called Mortol. It's like a puzzle platformer where, instead of lives, you have a spaceship full of little men, and each one sacrifices his life to progress everyone else. I just thought the design work was insane, and I spent an entire year playing the game, and I decided to give every title its due.

I think it's easily my favourite game of the last 20 years. I have golden in every cartridge, and I've cherry'd most cartridges. I speedrun a few of them, and one of the titles is Planet Zoldath, so hours can clock up when you're speedrunning.

My favourite is a game called Mini and Max, and it's a game about a little girl trapped in a closet, and the entire game takes place in this walk-in closet. But she learns through the help of her dog—who can talk to her, of course—that she can shrink herself down, or at least use her imagination to pretend she's shrinking herself down, and so the game takes place at a minuscule scale within the closet …. Without spoiling too much about this game, I have a massive, 100-page notebook for the game where I was just mapping out things to a micro scale.

My official recommendation, as someone who had an amazing experience … is boot it up and just start chronologically. Act like you're a kid who only gets one game a week, and just play that game until you want to give up on it, but maybe try to play it a little longer than your instincts.

What game will you never, ever uninstall?

(Image credit: Sierra)I think it would have to be something that would be inconvenient to reinstall … there's a few borderline abandonware games that I remember having to jump through hoops to actually play again. One at the top of my mind is a game called Lighthouse: The Dark Being. I think it's by Sierra, and it's a first-person, point-and-click, post-Myst exploration game.

It's not the most amazing game in the genre. There were a lot of post-Myst point-and-click adventure games of various quality levels. But I was one I was fond of as a kid, and it's one that was technically difficult to play, at least when I tried to play it.

The work of Michael Brough, actually, his game Cinco Paus is not on Steam, and that's one of my all-time game experiences. I think you can download it from itch. These are games I used the executable files on, as opposed to using Steam. I'll say Cinco Paus too. I won't uninstall Cinco Paus.

What's a piece of non-gaming software installed on your PC that you simply couldn't live without?

Adobe Photoshop. It's the software I know the best, and the one I'm technically the most fluent in, having used it daily since 1999.

It's the one piece of software I've used across all my creative pursuits in my career. It's my canvas when I paint. I use it for motion graphics, for compositing work. It's the foundation of all my web design for all the websites I've made throughout the years. For game design, obviously, all the graphics in Blue Prince, and even for niche stuff like DVD menus, which was actually my first job when I moved to Hollywood.

I'm not into a lot of the changes over the last few years. Obviously, all the AI integration. I just want to stick on, essentially, because I developed all those skills. I'm really comfortable in the 2019 model, right before they moved to the subscription.

How tidy is your desktop screen?

Tonda Ros sitting at his battle station, circa 1999. (Image credit: Tonda Ros)For my workstation, it's a bit of a mess. I basically never see my desktop as my monitors are eternally occupied with various game dev software that I never shut down. Unity and Photoshop pretty much have 100% uptime. I don't shut my computer down when I go to sleep, so when I get back up, I resume exactly where I left off, just get right back into it. So that's always dominating my screen real-estate, so I don't have too much incentive to keep it clean.

However, on my dedicated Steam machine, which is a mini PC that I use to game on the couch, that desktop is kept really clean, because I don't want anything on that PC that's not software that I need to run games. On that desktop, it's just a shortcut to Steam, an executable file of Cinco Paus, and one Chrome shortcut to a random Kyle Bosman video playing his Happy Monday song, which I play every Monday for my pet bunny.

I have no idea why, but that bunny gets so excited when he hears the piano at the start of that song, and it's the only music he's ever responded to.

Can we see your pet bunny?
