blocks.x: Disk Cleanup

(Image credit: Future)Welcome to Disk Cleanup, our regular weekend feature delving into the PCs of PC gaming luminaries. Come back every weekend to read a new interview, digging into the important questions, like "How tidy is your desktop?" and "What game will you never uninstall?"

Tonda Ros was first drawn to PC gaming at seven years old, after playing the action-adventure classic, Beast. "It's kind of like an open, nonlinear Sokoban that's action-based and not puzzle-based," says Ros, the creator of 2025's Blue Prince. "I think it was the next year where we had a 386 PC in the house, and that's when the floodgates opened … when I played Tank Wars and the original SimCity and Star Control."

Establishing a career as a cinematographer and visual artist, in 2016, Ros began working on Blue Prince. Inspired by games like Myst, board games like Jewels in the Attic and puzzle books like Maze: Solve the World's Most Challenging Puzzle, Blue Prince was painstakingly created across the best part of a decade. When it released last year, it quickly established itself as a modern puzzling classic.

After taking a break following Blue Prince's launch, Ros is currently working on tech support for the puzzler, while also experimenting with new projects. "I think the next game will have to be a smaller game, logistically," he says. But he stepped out of his game development lab to show me around the ever-shifting parlour of his Steam library.
What game are you currently playing?

(Image credit: The Game Bakers)I'm currently playing Cairn, by The Game Bakers, which is just a gorgeous rock-climbing simulator/adventure game with some survival elements. What's remarkable about the game is how much it feels like rock climbing, and how simple and intuitive the controls are.

I didn't even have to do a tutorial to understand, because that's just how simple and intuitive the controls are—where you control each limb in sequential order. It's just one of the most well-executed control schemes that I've ever seen. And it's not a control scheme that I had seen before.

I think what's really interesting to me is how similar the controls are, conceptually, to last year's Baby Steps, because these are both games where you're controlling individual limbs [and] climb up a mountainous terrain. But one is incredibly intuitive and smooth and frictionless—in the way the controls are executed at least. And then of course Baby Steps goes to the opposite side of the metric.
I love both games, and I think it's cool to see such similar design work conceptually, but with just slight tweaks in the game feel, they're completely different and unique experiences.
What was the previous game you played, and is it still installed?

(Image credit: Panic)That would be Big Walk, which is funny because that's also a game about climbing and walking. But yes, I just finished—two weeks ago—Big Walk with my group of friends, and that was an amazing experience.

I have been waiting for that game since it was announced at The Game Awards many years ago, and it's fascinating, because it's the first social proximity chat game I've ever played. I had been waiting for Big Walk for so long that every time other ones came up, I was like, "Yeah, I'd like to play this, but I'm waiting for Big Walk."

It's fascinating because they started development before this whole social chat scene kicked in. It reminds me a lot of Blue Prince, because I started Blue Prince's development before there were any deckbuilders. So you kind of get a sense that this is something that was created in parallel to those design trends, and you see the different decisions that they made, in the same way that I don't think Blue Prince really feels like a deck builder, though you could probably tell we share similar tabletop designs.

I played it with [seven] people. We had been prepped to play this for years … we played it on Thursdays and Sundays, Thursday was a shorter session and then Sunday was a little bit longer. And it was fun because seven people really allowed us to get lost in groups, where two people would be in a conversation and get distracted and fall away, and we wouldn't see them again for four hours. And that was exciting to me.

I don't want to spoil Big Walk for anyone that plays, but the ending just blew me away. I will say that it literally shook me. I think for a lot of times, I'm playing as a game designer, and you can't help but have a little design hat on where you're like "Oh, I would have done this differently" or "I think I could see ways that they could have improved this."

And when I played the last act of Big Walk, I was in awe, because there is no way I could have come to a fraction as good of an ending to that game, as the way they did. So hats off to House House, well deserved success.
What is the oldest game (by release date) currently installed on your PC?

I had thought it would be this, and I'm happy to report it's Myst, 1993. I have Cyan's entire catalogue installed. Myst will always be on my PC. It might not always be the oldest, but Myst is not one that's going anywhere.

There were many, many years where I just liked hanging out in that world, just to listen to the atmosphere while I was working. Hearing the wind and the oceans lap at the shore of Myst island. It has a serene quality. And it has a very deep familiarity because of how many years of my life were spent in that game as a kid, and especially [because] it was my first exposure to an immersive graphical world.

The very first time I played Myst was at a friend's house, and I was going to check out their Super Nintendo because they had just gotten [one] around the same time, and then he was like "Do you want to play something else?" And he took me to his father's office, who had a PC on his desk, and he booted it up, and I was just absolutely stunlocked … and I remember the day I got back, I told my parents—I didn't ask for a Super Nintendo—I told them "We need to get a computer with a CD-ROM."

I'm glad that my game and Big Walk and these games are finding success … because unlike a lot of other genres that are oversaturated, the first-person puzzle game is really not oversaturated. It's crazy, because you have Outer Wilds and Obra Dinn and all these games finding success and [being] universally beloved, and the community is ravenous for new experiences … I hope it encourages more people to explore these areas.
What is the highest number of hours you have in any given game, according to Steam?

(Image credit: Mossmouth)I'm only looking at Steam here, so thankfully I get to discount Battle.net, and I'm going to disqualify my own game. So the winner would be Mossmouth's magnificent UFO 50, clocking in at 691 hours. But I'm pretty sure a few hundred of those hours are because of Pilot Quest, which likely won't surprise anyone familiar with the game.

If you aren't familiar … UFO 50 is a collection of 50 games—so it's kind of a cheat in terms of the hours—that all belong to a fictional 1980s console called the LX. And if my hours of play are any indication, these are not 50 mini games. They're 50 games, full games that have a lot of depth, and they're as sizeable as any of the games from the '80s.

There are games across every genre. I remember when I first heard of it, I was like, "OK, that's a cool concept, [but] I don't really play a lot of retro nostalgia-driven games." But when I first saw a clip, the design work I was seeing was like, "Oh, they're doing some cool stuff." I think I saw a clip of one of the games called Mortol. It's like a puzzle platformer where, instead of lives, you have a spaceship full of little men, and each one sacrifices his life to progress everyone else. I just thought the design work was insane, and I spent an entire year playing the game, and I decided to give every title its due.

I think it's easily my favourite game of the last 20 years. I have golden in every cartridge, and I've cherry'd most cartridges. I speedrun a few of them, and one of the titles is Planet Zoldath, so hours can clock up when you're speedrunning.

My favourite is a game called Mini and Max, and it's a game about a little girl trapped in a closet, and the entire game takes place in this walk-in closet. But she learns through the help of her dog—who can talk to her, of course—that she can shrink herself down, or at least use her imagination to pretend she's shrinking herself down, and so the game takes place at a minuscule scale within the closet …. Without spoiling too much about this game, I have a massive, 100-page notebook for the game where I was just mapping out things to a micro scale.

My official recommendation, as someone who had an amazing experience … is boot it up and just start chronologically. Act like you're a kid who only gets one game a week, and just play that game until you want to give up on it, but maybe try to play it a little longer than your instincts.

(Image credit: Sierra)I think it would have to be something that would be inconvenient to reinstall … there's a few borderline abandonware games that I remember having to jump through hoops to actually play again. One at the top of my mind is a game called Lighthouse: The Dark Being. I think it's by Sierra, and it's a first-person, point-and-click, post-Myst exploration game.

It's not the most amazing game in the genre. There were a lot of post-Myst point-and-click adventure games of various quality levels. But I was one I was fond of as a kid, and it's one that was technically difficult to play, at least when I tried to play it.

The work of Michael Brough, actually, his game Cinco Paus is not on Steam, and that's one of my all-time game experiences. I think you can download it from itch. These are games I used the executable files on, as opposed to using Steam. I'll say Cinco Paus too. I won't uninstall Cinco Paus.
What's a piece of non-gaming software installed on your PC that you simply couldn't live without?
Adobe Photoshop. It's the software I know the best, and the one I'm technically the most fluent in, having used it daily since 1999.

It's the one piece of software I've used across all my creative pursuits in my career. It's my canvas when I paint. I use it for motion graphics, for compositing work. It's the foundation of all my web design for all the websites I've made throughout the years. For game design, obviously, all the graphics in Blue Prince, and even for niche stuff like DVD menus, which was actually my first job when I moved to Hollywood.

I'm not into a lot of the changes over the last few years. Obviously, all the AI integration. I just want to stick on, essentially, because I developed all those skills. I'm really comfortable in the 2019 model, right before they moved to the subscription.
How tidy is your desktop screen?

Tonda Ros sitting at his battle station, circa 1999. (Image credit: Tonda Ros)For my workstation, it's a bit of a mess. I basically never see my desktop as my monitors are eternally occupied with various game dev software that I never shut down. Unity and Photoshop pretty much have 100% uptime. I don't shut my computer down when I go to sleep, so when I get back up, I resume exactly where I left off, just get right back into it. So that's always dominating my screen real-estate, so I don't have too much incentive to keep it clean.

However, on my dedicated Steam machine, which is a mini PC that I use to game on the couch, that desktop is kept really clean, because I don't want anything on that PC that's not software that I need to run games. On that desktop, it's just a shortcut to Steam, an executable file of Cinco Paus, and one Chrome shortcut to a random Kyle Bosman video playing his Happy Monday song, which I play every Monday for my pet bunny.
I have no idea why, but that bunny gets so excited when he hears the piano at the start of that song, and it's the only music he's ever responded to.

items.author: Jacob Fox
items.summary:
Jacob Fox, hardware writer

(Image credit: Future)This week I've been: trying out the X3 Superstrike and Sensei Pro gaming mice, as well as a new Logitech
items.text:
Jacob Fox, hardware writer

(Image credit: Future)This week I've been: trying out the X3 Superstrike and Sensei Pro gaming mice, as well as a new Logitech Hall effect keyboard.

What comes to mind when I say 'big brand competitive gaming mouse'? If you're anything like me, that particular Rorschach test will make you spit out the word 'expensive.' That response isn't wrong, either: just look at the big releases we've had this year.

There was the Logitech G Pro X2 Superstrike: $180. The Razer Viper V4 Pro: $160. The SteelSeries Rival Pro and Sensei Pro: each $180. And there's an X3 Superstrike now, too, which is $200. These are some very expensive mice.

In previous years, I would have taken a dimmer view of this. Especially given the impressively competitive rodents you can pick up from niche Chinese brands these days. The $89 Mchose K7 V2 Ultra+, for example, is a Razer Viper V3/V4 Pro clone that performs very well and is plenty comfy.

And to be honest, even if fancy big brand mice are top-tier build quality, it's still a heck of a lot of money to ask for. The Rival Pro, Sensei Pro, and Viper V4 Pro specifically are truly fantastic on the build quality front, with the latter being practically flawless and cheaper than the rest, but they're all still very expensive.

So why isn't my view quite as dim as it could be? Because all of these releases have pushed the competitive gaming mouse scene forward in a way that probably only big brands can—both in terms of being able to absorb risk and also get new tech into as many hands as possible with big marketing campaigns.

In the case of Logitech, we have probably the most radical tech of all three: haptic-inductive (analogue) clicks. Then there's Razer, which has changed the way the sensor reports its data to save battery. And SteelSeries offers a few new things: primarily ultra-wideband (UWB) wireless connectivity and some changes to how it does polling (there are hot-swappable batteries, too, but those aren't completely new).

Logitech - analogue clicks

Analogue clicks let you adjust where the mouse button actuates, meaning you can have less time between deciding to click and actually clicking. It also lets you use rapid trigger, where you can re-click your mouse button as soon as you start to lift up on your previous click.

Razer - FrameSync

FrameSync is a technology that syncs up the mouse sensor's snapshots with when its microcontroller hands off that data to your PC. This means fewer sensor snapshots are required to maintain the same responsiveness, which ultimately saves battery.

SteelSeries - UWB and "true" 8K

Ultra-wideband (UWB) lets your mouse connect to its dongle wirelessly over different frequency bands to the usual ones, supposedly improving reliability. "True" 8K refers to how, at 8 kHz polling, the mouse doesn't batch together data but sends one packet for one receipt.

Logitech's analogue clicks

(Image credit: Logitech)Logitech's Haptic Inductive Trigger System (HITS) combines, well, haptics and induction, of course. The result is the ability to change how much you need to press down your mouse button before it actuates and registers a click, with the haptics there to ensure you get the feeling of a click wherever you set it to.

(Image credit: Future)Read more about the technology underneath the Superstrike

Logitech was the first to market with this tech. In fact, the company's head of engineering told me, "We knew we had a golden nugget in our hands... so we took all the shortcuts we could." Which probably goes some way towards explaining why an improved X3 Superstrike was released just seven months later—a fact that must surely sting some early X2 Superstrike buyers.

Since Logitech launched the X2 earlier in the year, we've seen that Keyhcron has been cooking up the "next gen mouse switch" which lets you choose between optical and magnetic within one switch, though its click feeling is static, meaning you won't be adjusting it to perfectly align with the actuation like with the Superstrike. We've also seen niche brand Finalmouse show off its TMR analogue clicks.

Razer's FrameSync

(Image credit: Razer)With the Viper V4 Pro, Razer introduced FrameSync—no, not Meta's FrameSync, something else. It essentially does for mice what VRR tech does for monitors, syncing up hardware with your system's polling. FrameSync ensures the mouse sensor's optical capture sync up with the microcontroller unit (MCU), ensuring it only captures the data when the MCU is polled by the PC and asks for it.

(Image credit: Future)Read more about how Razer's FrameSync technology works

One benefit is potentially to latency and jitter, but a good sensor doesn't really struggle with those things anyway. The actual benefit is to battery life, for one simple reason: there are fewer sensor snapshots required. That's how the Viper V4 Pro manages up to 180 hours of battery life at 1 kHz polling, despite the very performant sensor.

As far as I'm aware, Razer is the only company offering this kind of tech (Motion Sync is different). And we've seen from independent testing that FrameSync is indeed doing what it says it does.

SteelSeries' UWB and "true" 8K

(Image credit: SteelSeries)SteelSeries was the last to the 2026 'new competitive mouse tech' party, and its new technologies aren't quite as exciting as the ones mentioned previously, but are still great additions to the competitive mouse industry's toolkit. The new SteelSeries mice have hot-swappable batteries, and they're done well, but it's not the first company to have done so. It's the other technologies in there that are the newer ones.

(Image credit: Future)Read more about the collection of new technologies in the Rival Pro and Sensei Pro

SteelSeries is the first company, as far as I'm aware, to use ultra-wideband (UWB) in a mouse, apart from niche Japanese brand Elecom, which announced a similar mouse just a few weeks prior. The UWB promise is for more stable and reliable wireless connectivity. SteelSeries is also offering "true" 8K, as it claims its polling doesn't bundle up data packets but sends one packet for one receipt. Elecom makes similar claims about its mouse. SteelSeries also lets you have a lower sensor polling rate than click polling rate, but I think sensor polling is more important so I'm not too fussed about that feature.

None of these technologies on their own are quite as exciting as haptic clicks or synced sensors, but if other brands follow suit and add similar features to their mice, I certainly won't be complaining.

Big brands risk it, others follow

(Image credit: Future)After learning about all that niche brands have to offer, such as Chinese ones that make 'clones' of well-known mice, I did wonder for a while whether big brands like Razer, Logitech, and SteelSeries can continue charging so much for theirs. After all, you really can get great-performing, comfy, well-built mice for much cheaper than these big companies charge for their own options.

Perhaps these big brands started wondering the same, and rather than charging less, instead decided to use their big bucks to take the risk of investing in developing new tech. I'm sure much of this was done selfishly—to have something new and shiny to offer that other brands don't—but the positive side-effect for us consumers is that these new technologies are sure to spread out across the industry.

We should remember that with all these gaming mice, the mouse makers themselves don't make all their internal components (though Logitech does design its own sensors). Sensors, switches, and the like, are usually made in collaboration with distinct manufacturers of those parts. Which means that the new mouse tech we've seen this year isn't likely to be wrapped up with just one brand forever, unless the companies have very deep hooks in patents and whatnot.

(Image credit: Future)The fact that it's the big brands that have been taking on the risk of developing and implementing new tech also has the benefit of giving these technologies a stamp of legitimacy plus widespread marketing. Not everyone is a competitive mouse enthusiast, and most probably won't try a niche brand's mouse tech, however good it might be.

But taking the Superstrike as a paradigmatic example, Logitech is a big enough brand and has put enough marketing into its haptic-inductive click tech that people generally now accept that the technology is legitimate, useful, and marketable. Thus why other brands haven't been scared to follow suit. No doubt it helps to have some working models in the wild to see exactly how to make it work technically well, too.

All of this is to say that yes, top-tier competitive mice from big brands are ridiculously expensive these days. And yes, I'd still recommend picking up one of the many cheaper but still-quality options out there instead if you don't have a big budget. But I also have to hand it to the big brands for actually pushing the industry forwards in a way that's likely to stick. Rising tides to raise all boats, y'know?

items.title: I'm not sure the "AI" in my chair's lumbar support actually counts as AI, but it has been smart enough to help my posture
items.author: Jon Martindale
items.summary: Note from James, 02/10: We've heard your complaints that some of the wording in this piece - a lot of which, if I'm honest, was added/changed by me in the edit
items.text:
Note from James, 02/10: We've heard your complaints that some of the wording in this piece - a lot of which, if I'm honest, was added/changed by me in the edit - overstates the chair's potential health benefits. The HBADA’s X7 chair may reduce back pain during long periods of sitting at your desk but it will not literally fix your spine. While it is and will remain the RPS way to indulge in some occasional hyperbole, we don't want to suggest that swivel chairs cure physical conditions, so I've clarified these bits to avoid confusion.

AI is everywhere, exhausting to keep up with, and increasingly perceived as harmful to games. But that’s mostly generative AI; the more limited, less media-scraping and energy-hungry breeds of artificial intelligence can still play a harmless, maybe even useful role, especially on the hardware side. Even if it finds itself in some unexpected places, as is the case with HBADA’s X7 chair.

While AI-powered lumbar support sounds like the kind of gimmicky nonsense that’s become all too common in 2026, I’ve been using an X7 for a week, and it’s... surprisingly effective? Definitely for straightening up my posture, which I'm hopeful will help with my recurring back pain issues. It’s been a very pleasant surprise.

Granted, it had better yield results for the price. The X7 is on an Autumn sale at the time of writing, and it’s still £1,169 - at a time when most of the PC components you’d use while sitting in it are historically expensive. Rightfully, it does at least throw the kitchen sink at its features list: 720-degree adjustable arm rests, a built-in footrest, a 4D adjustable headrest, an "8D bionic" back massager, a "cloud ventilated" seat cushion with cooling fans, and a "graphene heating and red light therapy," system all come as standard.

Considering the bevy of buzzwords and baubles, I was extremely sceptical of HBADA’s "Automotive grade", AI-based smart lumbar system. Surely nobody actually needs an artificial intelligence to manage the placement of their lumbar support. And even if they did, what would it actually do?

As it turns out, the X7’s application of machine learning is high-tech for a chair, but relatively simple by today’s AI standards. The automatic adjustment works by, firstly, using magnetic sensors to detect the amount of pressure you’re placing on the lumbar support at any given time. The chair then reacts accordingly, either retracting the lumbar support, or extending it. Again, it feels more like old-fashioned sensors and motors than an artificial intelligence at work, but work it most certainly does.

One catch is that it can also support bad posture, especially at its stiffer setting. If I slump down in the chair, or don’t push myself back into the seat properly, it’ll hold me up in something approximating comfort. But that’s a terrible posture to maintain, and if I stay there too long I’m going to do my middle-age back some real harm that no expensive chair, AI-aided or otherwise, is going to fix.

I wish it could go a little lower, as I tend to get knots closer to my pelvis, but it’s still a nice addition. The heating element also works with it in tandem, and the fact that both engage automatically after a period of time is great when I’m in the mouse-and-keyboard zone and therefore not paying close attention to my back health.

The seat-mounted fans are a little loud, especially at higher settings. But assuming British summers in the mid-thirties Celsius really are the new normal, I can see these coming in real handy in a sweaty office full of high-wattage gaming gear. The lean-back auto-tensioning is too loose to really use it unlocked, too, and the headrest is quite wieldy. Compared to the rest of the chair, it seems clunky and imprecise. I don’t need another AI motor system there, but it stands out compared to the rest as rather basic and unnecessary.

The former is genuinely useful in a way that I really didn’t think it would be, and although it has the scent of AI gimmickry about it - I don’t know if HBADA would even bother to call it "AI", were it not the 2026 fashion to do so – it is smarter than any lumbar support I’ve used in the past. The most comfortable, too, and certainly the most reactive.

For a home office drone like me, who spends a lot of time standing to avoid potential back issues, the X7 has been good for both my posture and my peace of mind. There’s still improvements that could be made, but if you want a chair that values your comfort above all else, the HBADA X7 is worth saving up for.

items.text:
Port Desire, the hemmed-in city setting of immersive sim No Law, is hard to place. At points, it reminds me of walking around Lisbon. It shares that Portuguese city's verticality, where hill-straddling streets shouldered by colourful houses and corner shops can feel like tiers on a wedding cake. The strong sunlight and bursts of foliage reinforce the mediterranean vibes. Yet, the port city's structure and history is much closer to Kowloon Walled City, the ungoverned Chinese enclave that existed within British-owned Hong Kong.

Through the 1900s, with the British government taking a hands-off policy to the tiny district and the Chinese government exercising no control over its citizens, Kowloon became the most densely populated city on earth, with 33,000 citizens living in just 2.6-hectare borders. With virtually no official police presence, the city attracted anyone looking for a less-observed, less-regulated life – gangs, refugees, and a surprising number of unlicensed dentists.

As one of No Law's creative directors, Tor Frick, tells it, Port Desire is very similar. Not specifically the dentists bit, more the general, isolated lawlessness.

Watch on YouTube

"The city is surrounded by deep seas and a border wall," Frick says. "This is a lawless city set between three neighbouring countries. This is like no man's land." There's a peacekeeping force that maintains the status quo and, as Frick puts it, "make sure it doesn't explode." None of the neighbouring countries wants to take over the city, but nor do they want it to disappear.

"This is a very convenient playground for all kinds of powers," Frick explains. "The neighbouring countries can do shady stuff here. There's illegal medical research, all kinds of vices and smuggling. This is a perfect scapegoat place."

Into that tinderbox, finely balanced on a tightrope above an open fire, you enter. Grey Harker, an ex-military hardcase just looking for the quiet life. Frick won't go into detail about exactly what happens at the start of No Law beyond saying "Essentially, you were wronged by the [city's] four mayors and you're going after them." From that fixed starting point, you are free to tackle the mayors in whatever you order you want.

Though, Frick says, the order you choose will "change their relationship to each other, their narrative, and also change the game systemically." He uses the example of finding a mayor who eats at a particular restaurant. Early in the game, they may be virtually undefended, but if you've knocked off a couple of their fellow magistrates and will find them much more heavily defended – "they know he's coming for them so they arm up."

But, this is getting away from what I saw of No Law – which didn't include any mayors or hint of the inciting incident that kicks off Harker's rampage through Port Desire. Instead Neon Giant co-founders Frick and Arcade Berg show off a lower stakes mission. There is a hotel and in that hotel is a room and in that room is a safe and in a safe is some intel that Harker needs. And they're going to show me two-ish different ways to get it.

The first approach is meant to be stealthy. Frick approaches the hotel forecourt, which is dotted with gang members whiling away their time patrolling and generally blocking the way to the front door. As he approaches the threshold of the forecourt he's warned to back off, which he does, but not before trying to pick the pockets of one of the guards. Now, Berg assures me this run was meant to be stealthy, but one of the other gang members spots Frick with his hands all up in his friend's business and sounds the alarm. The gang comes on in a wave, wielding clubs, throwing grenades, and generally being mighty violent. Frick takes them down with a taser and grenades of his own.

With the gang subdued rather than stealthed past, Frick enters the hotel.

On the second playthrough, which was supposed to be the violent one, Frick shows me what he would have done the first time. He piles up some crates next to a blind spot on the forecourt perimeter, climbs up them and hops from the teetering tower to a ledge that runs along the back of the yard. He crouch walks along that, behind where the guards obliviously stand about chatting, and drops down next to the front door to the hotel.

Inside, Frick is met by a receptionist who looks like they would be more at home on the Sopranos than Mad Men. Commenting on the commotion outside, Renn, the heavyset mobster behind the desk, refuses to let Harker through the locked door into the hotel block without a password. Back on playthrough one, Frick gets to searching around the lobby and in the adjoining laundry room, finds a piece of paper with the password written down. He gives it to the receptionist and is waved on through. In the second playthrough, Frick just shoots them in the head and pops round the desk to unlock the door himself.

To confuse this back and forth structure I've adopted for this write up further, there is also a hypothetical third playthrough. Earlier in the demo, Frick and Berg told me that every named character in the game has a home somewhere in Port Desire's open world. So I ask what would happen if I visited Renn at his home ahead of the mission and killed them there. "Well, then you could take the key from him in his apartment," Frick says. "There are plenty of cases like that. You can't sequence-break the game because it's built to not have a sequence." He then expands it out, saying "If you know where one of the mayors is you could just go there. It's not going to be easy necessarily, because often he's heavily guarded, but it is possible. Especially as you know more about the games. We want people to try and outsmart the game. It's a single player game, so if you managed to find some combination that is over the top, hilariously overpowered, cool. It's not competitive. If you have figured something out you should be rewarded."

Okay, leave that hypothetical playthrough behind, we're now back on the sneaky playthrough, Frick climbs the stairs, sneaks past two guards, and lockpicks his way into one of the rooms. Accessing the room immediately nets him some XP. Berg is keen to point out that it's not the lockpicking that earned the XP, but accessing the room itself. Neon Giant don't want to incentivise particular kinds of actions – lockpicking your way into the room, climbing in through an open window, or blowing the door off its hinges are all equally valid approaches. "There is no wrong way to play the game," Frick adds. As if to emphasise this point, on the violent play through, Frick snaps the neck of one of the guards and shoots the other in the face.

Guards avoided/disposed of and room accessed, Frick goes through the safe, nabs the intel and leaves the hotel through a window. On the sneaky playthrough where he accidentally killed all the guards, Frick is free to walk straight through the forecourt. On the violent playthrough where he was sneaky, Frick throws a grenade into the forecourt and it explodes into a bubble of slow time, making every enemy caught inside move like they leave in a world of treacle. He kills them all while they struggle to make sense of the bubble of slow-mo they're trapped within. Considering up until now I'd seen lockpicks, tasers, and handguns, this hints at a whole other sci-fi side to the armoury you can acquire.

I left the No Law presentation deeply impressed by what I saw. Its densely detailed, systemic sci-fi world reminded me of Arkane's best work, Hitman, and Cyberpunk 2077. Neon Giant say the game is the work of just 24 people, and it's hard to believe because similar games come from much larger teams. Still, in the weeks since I saw the game, I've read other previews of No Law and it's clear the playthroughs were tightly controlled. We were all shown the two runs of the same mission (though, it seems only mine descended into an accidental gun battle). I wouldn't read too much into this – in a busy conference you need to have some control over what a journalist sees – but, it means I'm reserving some judgement on just how much systemic variety No Law provides until we can play it for ourselves.

And you should know that I will be going from door to door in No Law's open-world, ransacking apartments and killing bouncers, just to see how much it breaks the game. I don't know if that approach should be labelled outsmarting, but I'll happily try and outdumb it.

Travel and accommodation to Gamescom was provided by the conference organisers.

The year might be drawing to a close, but it's a perfect time to do something new with your Japanese study! Take a look below at the latest list of Japanese learning resources, lovingly selected by our team, to help supercharge your Japanese study.

Activate Your Japanese!

Activate Your Japanese! is a 24-episode drama about a Vietnamese girl named Xuan who came to Japan to work in a hotel. It comes from Japan's national broadcasting network, known as NHK, which is known for producing quality video content about all sorts of topics. You can think of them as the BBC or CNN of Japan. In the drama, she encounters a sentient keychain, new friends, and lots of new Japanese. And as with any drama, there are elements of humor and romance that really make it entertaining.

Each video is divided into parts: The main skit, Today's Strategy, Onomatopoeia, and Welcome to My Japan. The main skit follows Xuan and her time adjusting to Japanese life, all while providing useful communication strategies. Next, the Today's Strategy section focuses on a useful communication strategy or phrase that Xuan utilized in the main skit. Plenty of examples are provided, making this part of each video particularly useful for learners. Then comes the Onomatopoeia bit, which introduces a common Japanese onomatopoeia. Again, several examples are provided to help reinforce how the word is used in real life. And finally, the Welcome to My Japan bit finishes off each video with a presentation of someone's life after coming to Japan. Many of these individuals immigrated to Japan for work and have lived in the country for several years. Their work, interests, and hobbies are highlighted in this section.

Every video in this series comes with translated captions and even a transcript, making it ideal for learners at level who want to practice reading or listening skills. But even if learning Japanese is not your main goal, the series can still be enjoyed purely as a drama for one's own entertainment. According to the site, this series will be available until 2027, so there's plenty of time to go through each of the 15-minute episodes.

Beyond Activate Your Japanese!, the NHK has a number of other resources for Japanese learners, like the Essential Japanese section, which provides survival phrases, and Easy Japanese: Conversation Lessons, which contains lots of learning content related to conversation practice. There's something for everyone, so check it out!

あかね的日本語教室

VIDEO

あかね的日本語教室, otherwise known as Akane's Japanese Class, is a popular YouTube channel produced by a Japanese teacher named Akane. This channel is targeted towards intermediate and advanced learners. However, Akane mentions that this channel is also accessible to beginners who want a bit of a challenge. The difficulty comes from all the videos being entirely in Japanese. The subtitles at the bottom of the screen are in Japanese, and include furigana over more difficult kanji. There are also closed captioning subtitles that can be turned off and on, with an impressive number of languages covered — 15!

The videos on this channel are very educational while also entertaining. The topics surround learning Japanese, travel around Japan, everyday life in Japan, and more. An example of Akane's videos that Japanese learners may find most useful are "[Business Japanese] Basics of telephone correspondence" and several interviews with non-native speakers living in Japan and studying the language. Each video lasts about 10-15 minutes in length, and they go by quickly. Because Akane speaks slowly, it's easy to follow the dialogue. If you're looking for even more content by Akane, you can also check out the podcast and Instagram page she also has.

Japanese Immersion with Asami

Japanese Immersion with Asami is a YouTube channel that, as the name suggests, focuses on teaching via comprehensible input; that is, Japanese made as easy to understand as possible, even for beginners, without relying on English explanations or translations. Asami has been a Japanese teacher since 2015, and with her trusty partner Hyougen, mostly reads stories in her videos, with helpful explanations and commentary; all in Japanese.

The videos are a great way to get your feet wet engaging with Japanese media more, without feeling like you're alone in the endeavor. In fact, the casual, supportive atmosphere of her videos might be their best feature; it really does feel like a private lesson. And with several series in a variety of genres and titles, such as Kiki's Delivery Service and short stories, you're sure to find a narrative that piques your interest.

日本語表現インフォ

One of the most difficult parts of learning another language can be expressions. As language conveys culture, each individual language has different expressions relevant to its own culture, and translating between them is no easy task. Thankfully for Japanese learners, there's the helpful website 日本語表現インフォ, or "Japanese Expression Info" to make things a little easier.

The site is very straightforward, with various expressions grouped into different categories, like expressions conveying emotions, sensations, or people, for example. From there they're often broken down even further, like expressions relevant to conveying different degrees of sadness.

While the website states the intent was to be a resource for people aiming to write in Japanese, it's helpful for Japanese learners as well. Not only will using these sorts of expressions add a sense of naturalness to your own writing, but they might help you while reading Japanese. 日本語表現インフォ is a great resource for learning both Japanese language and culture.

Sail

Sail is a unique approach to Japanese language exchange apps. Available on iOS and Android, Japanese learners first register for an account, filling out some of their interests and a basic self-introduction. But rather than connect with teachers or other language learners, Sail connects you to native Japanese speakers in the form of retirees and senior citizens. Like all similar apps, you're able to look at the profiles of various exchange partners, and find someone who might be a good fit in terms of interests and availability. Conversations are set to last 25 minutes, offering a contained experience: long enough that you're able to actually chat, but not so long that you might run out of steam.

It's a unique concept, and one that works well. Older people make good conversation partners, and are often very cordial and have a lot of free time. They're excited to get the chance to connect to learners, and share something of their language and culture, and this eagerness is contagious. What's even better is that Sail allows for unlimited conversations for a simple fee of $14.90 a month, with discounts at longer terms. This makes Sail one of the best bangs for your buck for Japanese learners hoping to converse.

パパパパパピィ

Update: Sadly this resource is no longer available.

Do you miss the good ol' days of reading picture books as a kid? Would you like to know more about Japanese children's books and the colorful images and themes they have inside? With the YouTube channel パパパパパピィ, you can read along, in a bedtime story fashion, to many different Japanese children's books.

Each story is read front to back by the host of the channel, who keeps you engaged with different voices and sounds, depending on the character or noise. You'll be able to follow along with the script, as the pages are shown while being narrated. Picture books are a great resource for beginner learners, as they don't have as many kanji. The readings are very short, witheach video being under ten minutes long. Whether you're looking to find more resources for your kids, or you're wanting to bring back the nostalgia of reading children's books, give this channel a go and watch how you're instantly transported to the land of cheery Japanese stories!

Megumi's Daily Japanese Adventures

If you're wanting to get more listening practice in, the podcast Megumi's Daily Japanese Adventures could be the right fit for you. This podcast was created for Japanese learners and could be used somewhat similarly to JLPT listening practice. In this podcast, the host, Megumi, talks about various experiences she's had related to travel, Japanese culture, and more. The way Megumi describes these adventures is story-like, with background music to accompany her anecdotes and detailed accounts. She speaks slowly and clearly, which is good for those who are just beginning to listen to content that's entirely in Japanese. The targeted audience for this podcast is around the intermediate level.

For listeners who would like to follow along with the dialogue, there are also transcripts on Megumi's website. At the end of these transcripts, there are English translations for some of the more advanced vocabulary. The episodes are around 5 minutes in length, so they're quick listens if you want to give them a go.

Human Japanese

Made by the same people who brought us Satori Reader, the Human Japanese apps are basically digital textbooks for Japanese, or as they call it, your "personal sensei in a box." There is an app for beginners and then an intermediate-level version. The beginner version boasts over 500 pages of content and around 800 example sentences, with breakdowns of each word and particle to boot! When teaching kana and kanji, there are stroke order animations, and plenty of example words as well.

The lessons in this app are truly worded and organized like a textbook. You will find lessons related to food, school, geography, health, work, and the weather. Major grammar points are included as well, including lessons on verbs, adjectives, adverbs, conjugations, counting, particles, and more. At the end of each lesson, you can find review quizzes. By default, you cannot move on to the next chapter until you have passed a chapter review quiz, but you can change this in the settings.

The overall design of the app is sleek and nice, but can feel a little dated to some seeing as it was originally created over a decade ago. Some pages are a little intimidating because of their word count, which some may find annoying. And there are no romaji to help you out; the app assumes you will learn hiragana and katakana. So if this kind of electronic textbook is just what you're looking for, then Human Japanese may be for you. For readers looking to give it a try, they offer a lite version free of charge.

YomuJP

For the Japanese graded reader junkies out there looking for more material, you might want to check out YomuJP. This website is dedicated to providing Japanese learners with easy, level-appropriate reading content in a simple layout.

There are tons of writings in their database. Each article contains pictures, and even audio recordings of a native speaker reading the material. This means you can use this site for listening practice as well. The stories are separated by reading difficulty. There are six categories, from N6 to N1, with N6 being the easiest (introductory level Japanese) and N1 being the hardest (advanced Japanese). According to the site, this scale is based on the Japanese Language Proficiency Test (JLPT) with N6 being an even easier level than the JLPT's lowest level of N5. You can browse articles by difficulty level or by tag.

The site also regularly posts to their Twitter page, often highlighting articles. New articles seem to be consistently released as well. If you are interested in practicing your reading (or listening) skills, or if you are thinking of studying for the JLPT, then consider YomuJP as one handy-dandy tool in your toolbox.

Thanks so much for following along with us to the end of the year, and the end of the article! We hope it's been a helpful journey. From all of us at Tofugu, hope you have a relaxing 正月, and spring is right around the corner.

items.text:
Bill Gurley spent years on Wall Street, built his career as a partner at Benchmark, worked through Uber’s hypergrowth era, and now serves on the board of the Santa Fe Institute, where he studies complexity and systems thinking.

Featured clips

Obsessive Learning in Founders

The Craft of Storytelling and Writing

Available Now: YouTube | Spotify | Apple Podcasts | Transcript | X

In this episode, Bill shares the mental models he returns to most often, including systems thinking, second- and third-order effects, and the importance of understanding both the bedrock of your field and the bleeding edge.

He explains what separates great founders, why storytelling and product instincts matter, how he uses AI across different models, and what he sees coming in open source, China, stablecoins, tokenization, payments, and venture capital.

+ Check out Runnin’ Down a Dream: How to Thrive in a Career You Actually Love

++ Check out the Granola Notes

Tiny Lessons

Trajectory matters more than the starting place.

“Success requires balancing a deep knowledge of history with an obsessive focus on the technological edge where disruption happens.”

“I think more people would benefit by studying the history of whatever field they’re in.”

“If it’s tedious to learn, it isn’t a passion. I don’t think you’re in the right lane.”

“I think that anybody in any field should want to be curious about the bleeding edge and what happens.”

“You should understand the really old stuff, the history, because it’s differentiating and shows a passion and it gives you a great frame of mind, but you also want to really understand the new edge. If you do both of those things, I think you’re a power player in your field.”

“If you have to write it out and make it stand alone and be cogent, you’ll think through more of the problems and it’ll be more cohesive and you’ll figure out the loose ends and you’ll tie them up.”

“If regulation gets extremely difficult and mundane and expensive, that could actually lead to more oligopoly.”

“I would describe complex systems as multivariable nonlinear systems. And multivariable nonlinear systems are very hard to predict. They can behave one way for a long time, and then one variable can switch and they can behave another way—the weather, stock markets, all these things. There are consequences that can be first, second, or third-order. You can’t just think with a linear model or just think about one variable because things can go way off the path. You need to be aware that if you make a change here, it could change something here, which could change something there, and it has to be the whole system.”

“You’ve got to be really conscious of the consequence and not get too deterministic about a single metric or a single variable.”

“I’ve always thought of Wall Street as the buyer of the product that venture capitalists create because the eventual liquidity is either an M&A (merger and acquisition) or an IPO (initial public offering).”

One question to ask before hiring or investing in someone: Is this person going to do this no matter what?

Mario Harik is the CEO of XPO, one of the largest logistics companies in the world.

For years, he was the protege of legendary entrepreneur Brad Jacobs (who built eight multibillion-dollar companies from scratch). Today, Mario leads 40,000 people with a management style shaped by what he learned. It’s a rare combination of smart capital allocation, discipline, deep listening, and a genuine belief in human potential.

Mario shares how he uses real-time data and second-order thinking to make better decisions faster, how he hires and develops A players (and the test that instantly tells you who isn’t one), how he runs meetings that pull the best thinking out of the most junior person in the room, what he learned working alongside one of the best entrepreneurs of our generation, and why ego, complacency, and small goals are quietly capping everything.

I hope you enjoy this conversation as much as I did.

Featured clips

Letting go of perfection and understanding how people operate

Learning from frontline employees and feedback loops

Analytical approach to risk and decision-making

Creating a high-performance environment through belief and feedback

items.text:
Humans have been slurping and savoring noodles for centuries, with the first recorded noodle dish recorded during China’s Eastern Han period (25–220 CE). In fact, noodles would go on to become inextricable from ancient Chinese culture, with a wheat-based version emerging as a staple of the Han dynasty. Centuries later, noodle-making would hit Europe, transforming the cuisines of Italy during the Middle Ages and Germany in the early 18th century. The English word “noodle” itself goes back to the 18th century, borrowed by the English from the German “nudel.”


Whatever you call them, one thing remains certain: Love of noodles transcends culture and country. Jacques Cousteau once said that the sea was “the great unifier ... man’s only hope,” but did he ever consider the power of a steaming bowl of ramen? For this delicious guide, we’ve noodled on the best of the best around the world—places where mind-bending broths and eccentric histories collide to create unforgettable dining experiences.

1. Hrimnir Ramen 📍 Oslo, Norway


This Oslo eatery puts a uniquely Norwegian spin on traditional Japanese ramen, using seasonal local ingredients found from the fjords to the mountains. Opened by Norwegian-American microbiologist David Quist in 2019, Hrimnir places a special focus on fermented ingredients, with jars of preserved lemons, pickled plums, and pear vinegar lining the walls. The noodles are handmade in house with emmer wheat or tokornkveite, a heritage grain that gives them a uniquely nutty flavor.

2. Phở Hàng Trống 📍 Hanoi, Vietnam


Hanoi is considered the birthplace of Vietnam’s staple noodle soup, phở, and in the living room of home chef Ms. Minh, you’ll find some of the very best in the country. She’s been selling phở in Hanoi for decades but was forced to take her business inside in 2017, when the city started cracking down on street vendors.


At plastic tables, visitors to Ms. Minh’s home can enjoy traditional, northern-style phở (which has lighter, clearer broth than that in the south). She serves her noodles with jars of homemade chili sauce and pickled garlic, plus the option of dipping Chinese youtiao doughnuts in the hot broth.


3. Inari Soba Mansei 📍 Tokyo, Japan


This small soba shop dates back to the early 1600s, where it appears in the legend of Takuzousu, a Buddhist monk and kitsune, or shapeshifting fox-spirit. It’s said that Takuzousu frequented this very shop, where the coins he paid with supposedly turned into leaves once their magic had worn off.


You’d never know the restaurant’s legendary history from the outside, but inside, you’ll find a bronze bell from the original Takuzousu shrine displayed in glass. The menu, too, pays tribute to the kitsune by serving aburaage, a fried tofu believed to be foxes’ favorite food.

4. Pekin Noodle Parlor 📍 Butte, Montana


Pekin Noodle Parlor is the oldest continuously-operating Chinese restaurant in the U.S., opened in 1911 in what was once a thriving Chinatown. Passed down through the same family for generations, Pekin radiates old-school charm: A flickering, neon sign welcomes visitors into a dimly-lit space with orange booths and individual eating cubicles, where food arrives by trolley. The parlor’s main draw is the Chinese-American classic, chop suey, but it also serves up a mean chow mein and chicken noodle soup.


5. Mie Lethek Garuda 📍 Srandakan, Indonesia


In this traditional factory, cows turn a huge mortar that grinds dried cassava and sweet potatoes into flour for mie lethek, the region’s signature noodle variety. Mie lethek translates to “ugly noodles,” an apt name for these squiggly gray creations. But what they lack in beauty, they make up for in flavor: sweeter than your average noodle, with a pleasant, chewy texture.


Yasir Feri, Mie Lethek Garuda’s owner, is the grandson of the noodle’s creators, a Yemeni/Chinese couple who first opened up shop in the 1940s. After the cows have created the flour, Feri and his factory workers mix and press the dough by hand, then leave the finished noodles to dry in the sun before bringing them to the market. (The cows are also given sweet grass in return for their hard work.)

6. Pure Love Diner Bar 📍 Taipei, Taiwan


Colorful neon signs welcome you into this ’80s-themed den of vice (and noodles), complete with red lighting, disco balls, and antique furniture. The diner is an homage to Taipei’s old-school karaoke bars, known as “grandpa shops” for their older—and often flirtatious—patrons, though without any of the original bars’ suspicious activity.


Here, it’s all about enjoying the kitschy ambiance and chowing down on Taiwanese classics like braised pork over rice, oyster soup, fried chicken, and deep-fried noodles in satay sauce. Plus, there’s still a karaoke machine in the corner!

7. Fideus de Vermar 📍 Binissalem, Spain


This small town of Binissalem celebrates its rich wine heritage with the annual Festa des Vermar, which includes (among plenty of wine-based activities) huge cauldrons of short noodles, slow-cooked meats, red wine, and aromatic spices. This traditional local paella, called fideus de vermar, serves all 1,400 of the town’s residents during the festival, turning the main square into a lively picnic spot.

8. Bamonte’s 📍 Brooklyn, New York


Founded by immigrants in 1900, this family institution holds the distinction of being Brooklyn’s oldest Italian restaurant. It was once a favorite meeting spot of the New York mafia, as well as a setting for the fictional New Jersey mob in “The Sopranos.” Other (more law-abiding) Italian-Americans of note, such as Robert De Niro and Frank Sinatra, have dined here, and the restaurant honors its many famous guests with framed photos on the walls.


While New York City has grown exceedingly expensive, Bamonte’s has kept its Italian classics surprisingly affordable, and crowd-pleasers like the rigatoni alla vodka and linguine with red clam sauce keep people coming back year after year.

9. Khanom Jeen Pa Mai 📍 Phuket Town, Thailand


Thin white rice noodles called khanom jeen are a staple throughout Thailand, where they’re served with various spicy curries, meats, and vegetables. At this unassuming eatery in Phuket Town, customization reaches new heights with a lineup of everything from crispy dried fish to pickled mustard greens to pineapple slices.

10. Hawker Chan Soya Sauce Chicken Rice & Noodle 📍 Singapore


For about $3, you can enjoy a Michelin-star meal at this Singapore noodle shop. Owner and chef Chan Hon Meng first opened Hawker Chan as a food-court stall, where it became famous with his “secret,” Cantonese-style chicken marinade. The flavorful braised meat is served over char siew noodles, rice, or hor fun noodles with stir-fried veggies and braised eggs.


After Meng took home a Michelin star in 2016 (which he at first assumed was a practical joke), he turned Hawker Chan into a full-scale restaurant right next to where his humble stall once stood. Since then, other locations have opened in Thailand, Kazakhstan, Laos, and Malaysia, with more still on the way.

11. Lin Heung Tea House 📍 Hong Kong


Founded in the late 19th century, Lin Heung may just be Hong Kong’s oldest dim sum spot. It still does things the old-school way, too, with servers wheeling trolleys stacked high with bamboo steamers and calling out what dishes are up. Simply head over to the trolley and load up on what looks good to you, whether it’s rice noodle rolls, shrimp dumplings, pork ribs, or congee. The tea house can get quite crowded, so sharing a table with (or even befriending) fellow customers is simply a part of the experience.

12. Matsuka Seimen Noodle Factory 📍 Kurashiki, Japan


This gray shed functions mainly as a noodle factory, but during certain times of day, it changes gears to serve up freshly-cooked udon topped with eggs, scallions, and chili oil. Regulars swear by the kamatama: piping hot udon paired with nothing but a raw egg (cooked by the noodles) and a drizzle of soy sauce. Matsuka Seimen’s tiny kitchen also churns out a rich curry ramen made with fatty slivers of pork and soba noodles in a delicate green tea broth.


If you’re lucky, while you wait for your meal, you’ll witness the Matsuka family’s rather unusual noodle-kneading technique: A large tray of dough is covered in cloth and placed on the floor, where a family member walks all over it in special socks.

13. Bún Riêu Gánh 📍 Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam


On the busy streets of Ho Chi Minh City, Mrs. Mai Thi Lien serves up hefty ladles of simmering red broth from a massive pot on the sidewalk. Bún riêu, the noodle soup for which her restaurant is named, is made with rice vermicelli noodles and shrimp or pork mixed with crab paste, plus crispy tofu, huyet (coagulated pork blood), and herbs for garnishing. Mrs. Lien puts her own spin on the classic dish by pairing it with a tamarind fish sauce with sliced chili, giving it a distinctly southern Vietnamese flavor.
